arXiv:2605.01342v1 [cs.DB] 02 May 2026

Don’t Be a Pot Stirrer! Authorized Vector Data Retrieval
via Access-Aware Indexing

Shanshan Han Affiliation: University of California, Irvine email: shanshan.han@uci.edu , Vishal Chakraborty Affiliation: University of California, Irvine email: vchakrab@uci.edu and Sharad Mehrotra Affiliation: University of California, Irvine email: sharad@ics.uci.edu
Abstract.

Vector databases increasingly enforce role-based access control: each top-kk approximate nearest neighbor query must return only vectors the querying role is authorized to access. Two extremes bracket the design space. A single global index avoids duplication but wastes search effort on unauthorized vectors and degrades recall, while an oracle index, built with all authorized vectors, searches only authorized vectors but duplicates every shared vector between roles or queries. We present Veda and its efficient variant EffVeda, two indexing strategies built on an access-aware lattice to address access control in vector databases. The methods first partitions the dataset into disjoint data blocks by role combination, then leverage the structure of the access-aware lattice to apply copy and merge operations to group co-accessed blocks under a user-specified storage budget. Large nodes in the lattice are then indexed with HNSW, while small nodes are retained for linear scan. For each role, our methods construct a query plan that selects the minimal set of nodes that covers the role’s authorized data. At query time, coordinated search first queries pure (authorized-only) nodes to populate a global top-kk heap. The resulting distance bound then prunes exploration on impure nodes, avoiding the inflated search that independent per-index execution would require.

1. Introduction

Vector databases now sit behind semantic search, recommendation, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020). Enterprise deployments increasingly hold data that not every user may see. A hospital’s RAG corpus, for instance, mixes clinical notes with billing records; a physician may read the former but not the latter, and an administrator the reverse. The retrieval layer must therefore enforce role-based access control (RBAC) (Bertino et al., 2011): a top-kk approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) query issued by role rr may return only vectors that rr is authorized to read. Regulations such as the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024) make this isolation a compliance requirement rather than an optional feature. Recall remains critical at the same time, since a clinical query that misses an authorized record can change a treatment decision.

A natural question is how to organize vector data with access control constraints so that queries can respect access policies while preserving high recall. Two extremes bracket the design space. A global index builds one ANN graph, e.g., HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018), over all vectors and discards unauthorized results after search. Storage stays minimal, but the search beam fills with vectors the role cannot access; recall drops, and the system must oversample to compensate. An oracle index is the ideal HNSW baseline that would be available if the query predicate were known at construction time (Patel et al., 2024). For a query with role rr, the oracle index builds an HNSW graph over exactly its accessible data. Every query then runs on a pure search index with no post-filtering or search-scope expansion, but every vector shared across mm roles is stored mm times. We measure this trade-off with two metrics.

Storage amplification (SA): the ratio of total indexed vectors to dataset size; the global index attains SA=1\textsf{SA}=1 and oracle indexing sets the upper bound.

Query amplification (QA): the average query cost normalized to oracle indexing; oracle indexing attains QA=1\textsf{QA}=1 and the global index sets the upper bound. The goal is an index layout near the lower-left corner of the SA–QA plane.

Prior work. A growing line of work folds attribute predicates into ANN search. Filtered-DiskANN (Gollapudi et al., 2023) adds label-aware edges to the Vamana graph so that traversal stays on points matching the query label. ACORN (Patel et al., 2024) expands each HNSW node’s neighbor list by a factor γ\gamma so that the predicate-matching subgraph remains navigable after filtering. They do not exploit the structure that RBAC imposes: a small fixed set of roles, union semantics over a user’s roles, and heavy overlap among role-authorized views. SIEVE (Li et al., 2025) and HoneyBee (Zhong et al., 2025) are data partitioning strategies that close to ours. SIEVE (Li et al., 2025) observes the historical workload and materializes a budget-bounded set of HNSW sub-indices for the most profitable filters, falling back to the global index for the rest. HoneyBee (Zhong et al., 2025) casts RBAC-aware indexing as constrained optimization and produces overlapping partitions that trade storage for latency. Two limitations remain. First, each role’s data must fit inside a single partition, so fine-grained overlap among roles cannot be exploited. Second, partitions are searched independently and merged afterward. When a partition is impure for role rr, i.e., it mixes vectors rr may and may not read, the search on that partition must inflate its beam to recover enough authorized candidates.

We argue that data partitioning is the natural fit for access-controlled ANN search. Three properties of RBAC make this so. (i) Access policies are dictated by organizational structure rather than by arbitrary attribute predicates, e.g., physicians read clinical notes, administrators read billing data, and a small public slice is shared. The data therefore admits a small, stable set of role-aligned partitions, unlike category filters (e.g., color, price) whose predicate combinations are unbounded. (ii) RBAC follows union semantics: a user’s view is the union of its roles’ authorized vectors, so a query is answered by unioning partition results rather than intersecting per-attribute indices. (iii) Policies evolve, such asdepartments merge, permissions are revoked, etc, and a partitioned layout absorbs such changes efficiently, whereas deleting a role’s vectors from a global HNSW graph can sever connectivity and force a full rebuild. Partitioning is not unconditionally optimal, however. When a query’s authorized region already covers most of the dataset, the query must touch many partitions and pay repeated index-switching and result-merging overhead. In this case, a single global index with in-search or post-search filtering is cheaper. We therefore treat the two as complementary: data partitioning serves selective queries, and a single global index serves broad ones. We exprimentally validate this crossover case with multi-role queries in Exp 13 in §7.

This paper. We present Veda and its efficient variant EffVeda, two indexing strategies built on an access-aware lattice. The lattice first splits the dataset into disjoint exclusive blocks, one per distinct role combination. Copy and merge operations then restructure the lattice under a user-specified SA budget β\beta. Copying a block into an ancestor spends budget but keeps both nodes pure to the accessed roles. Merging spends no budget but introduces impurity. Veda greedily picks the operation with the highest query-cost reduction per unit of added storage. EffVeda reaches a comparable layout faster by traversing the lattice bottom-up with deterministic heuristics that avoid re-scoring every candidate pair. Nodes that reach the indexability threshold Λ\Lambda are indexed with HNSW to support fast ANN search. Smaller nodes are kept as leftover vectors for linear scan, since linear scan beats HNSW at small sizes (§2.3). For each role we derive a query plan that selects a minimal set of nodes whose union covers that role’s authorized data. We pair the lattice with coordinated search, a query-execution procedure that shares state across the indices in a role’s plan. The procedure first scans leftovers and queries pure indices to fill a global top-kk heap. The kk-th distance in that heap then bounds the search on each impure index: an uninflated probe runs first, and the search inflates only if its kk-th local candidate beats the global bound. Coordinated search thus pays the inflation cost only on impure indices that can actually improve the result, and the mechanism is orthogonal to the partitioning strategy itself. We develop the partitioning strategy for single-role queries, and extend the evaluation to multi-role queries in Exp 13 in §7.

Contributions. We make the following contributions.

∙\bullet We formalize access-controlled ANN indexing as optimizing QA under an SA budget and introduce the access-aware lattice that exposes copy and merge as the two primitive operations on RBAC data (§3).

∙\bullet We present Veda, a greedy lattice-optimization algorithm (§4), and EffVeda, a bottom-up variant that reaches comparable layouts at lower construction cost (§5).

∙\bullet We introduce coordinated search that uses a global top-kk heap to prune exploration on impure indices while preserving recall (§6).

∙\bullet Evaluations show that Veda and EffVeda achieve high QPS at high recall while tracking the desired SA closely (§7).

Roadmap. §2 reviews HNSW and defines impurity and query cost under access control. §3 formalizes the index-selection problem and the exclusive lattice. §4 and §5 present Veda and EffVeda. §6 describes query planning and coordinated execution. §7 reports experiments, §8 surveys related work, and §9 concludes.

2. Role-Based Access Via Indices

This section lays the groundwork for access-control-aware indexing. §2.1 reviews HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018) (full details in Appendix §A). §2.2 defines index impurity under role-based access control, formalizes the query-cost model, and walks through four indexing strategies on a concrete example. §2.3 distills three design challenges that motivate Veda and EffVeda.

2.1. HNSW Overview

HNSW organizes vectors in a multi-layer proximity graph: upper layers hold sparse long-range links and lower layers hold dense short-range links (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018). A top-kk query enters at a random node on the top layer and greedily descends toward closer neighbors until it reaches the bottom layer. Search on the bottom layer expands each candidate node’s neighbors through a priority queue PQ of capacity 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} and returns the kk closest entries. In practice, 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} is a query-time beam width chosen to be at least kk and tuned for the desired recall–latency trade-off. We set 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} to α​k\alpha k, where α\alpha is a small constant (typically 55–1010 in practice (Johnson et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Aumüller et al., 2020)). For instance, a top-1010 query on 𝐱\mathbf{x} retains 𝖾𝖿𝗌∈[50,200]\mathsf{efs}\in[50,200] candidates in the priority queue PQ. The implicit assumption is that the true top-kk neighbors of 𝐱\mathbf{x} appear among these 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} candidates with high probability. We state it formally.

Assumption 0 (HNSW Search Accuracy).

Let 𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}({\tt idx}) be the set of vectors stored in an HNSW index 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx}, and let q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) be a top-kk query for the nearest neighbors of 𝐱\mathbf{x} accessible to role rr. Let PQ be the priority queue of capacity 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} maintained during search on 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx}. With high probability, dist​(𝐱,v)<dist​(𝐱,v′)\textsf{dist}(\mathbf{x},v)<\textsf{dist}(\mathbf{x},v^{\prime}) for all v∈PQv\in\textsf{PQ} and v′∈𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)∖PQv^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}({\tt idx})\setminus\textsf{PQ}.

Asymptotic Query Cost. Let 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} be an HNSW index and let MM denote the number of neighbors inspected per node during traversal. A top-kk HNSW query has the standard comparison-based bound

𝒪⁡(M​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+M​𝖾𝖿𝗌​log⁡𝖾𝖿𝗌+𝖾𝖿𝗌​log⁡k),\mathcal{O}\!\left(M\log|{\tt idx}|+M\mathsf{efs}\log\mathsf{efs}+\mathsf{efs}\log k\right),

where the terms correspond to upper-layer descent, base-layer beam search, and final top-kk extraction. Since kk is small in our setting (top-11 to top-55 passages usually suffice for LLM inference (Reichman and Heck, 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023)), the extraction term is negligible; dropping the constant MM for the log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|\log|{\tt idx}| and 𝖾𝖿𝗌​log⁡𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs}\log\mathsf{efs} terms gives 𝒪⁡(log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+𝖾𝖿𝗌​log⁡𝖾𝖿𝗌)\mathcal{O}(\log|{\tt idx}|+\mathsf{efs}\log\mathsf{efs}). To use this bound as a comparable cost proxy, we keep the two surviving features and make the hidden constants explicit: Cθcmp​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,𝖾𝖿𝗌)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+b​𝖾𝖿𝗌​log⁡𝖾𝖿𝗌+c,C^{\textsf{cmp}}_{\theta}({\tt idx},\mathsf{efs})=a\log|{\tt idx}|+b\,\mathsf{efs}\log\mathsf{efs}+c, where θ=(a,b,c)\theta=(a,b,c) are fitted coefficients for upper-layer traversal, base-layer search, and fixed per-query overhead. Definition 2.2 below gives the deployment-calibrated latency model used by our algorithms.

2.2. Access-Control-Aware Indexing

To enforce access control with HNSW, we partition the dataset into groups and build one HNSW index per group. A group may hold vectors from several roles, so an index can be impure for a given role rr: it stores vectors that rr is not authorized to read.

Definition 2.1 (Pure and Impure Indices).

An index 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} is pure with respect to role rr if every vector it stores is authorized for rr; otherwise 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} is impure. Let 𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}({\tt idx}) denote all vectors in 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} and 𝒟r​(𝚒𝚍𝚡)⊆𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}_{r}({\tt idx})\subseteq\mathcal{D}({\tt idx}) the subset authorized for rr.

We quantify impurity as

(1) λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r=⌈|𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)||𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)∩𝒟⁡(r)|⌉,\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}=\left\lceil\frac{|\mathcal{D}({\tt idx})|}{|\mathcal{D}({\tt idx})\cap\mathcal{D}(r)|}\right\rceil,

where 𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)∩𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}({\tt idx})\cap\mathcal{D}(r) is the subset of 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} accessible to rr. To compensate, the retrieval target is inflated from kk to λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r​k\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}\,k and 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} is inflated from α​k\alpha k to α​λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r​k\alpha\,\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}\,k. The priority queue thus grows linearly with impurity, and more candidates must be examined to maintain recall. Where unambiguous we write λ\lambda for λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}.

Definition 2.2 (Cost of Role-Based Queries on HNSW).

Let 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} be an HNSW index with size |𝚒𝚍𝚡||{\tt idx}|, let 𝖾𝖿𝗌=α​k\mathsf{efs}=\alpha k, and let

Cθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,𝖾𝖿𝗌)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+b​𝖾𝖿𝗌+cC_{\theta}({\tt idx},\mathsf{efs})=a\log|{\tt idx}|+b\,\mathsf{efs}+c

be the latency model fitted on the target hardware for 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} searched with beam width 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs}. The cost of a top-kk query issued by role rr on 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} is denoted CostH\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}, where H denotes HNSW:

CostH​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,r)={Cθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,𝖾𝖿𝗌),if ​𝚒𝚍𝚡​ is pure w.r.t. ​rCθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,⌈λ​𝖾𝖿𝗌⌉),if impure and ​λ​𝖾𝖿𝗌≤|𝚒𝚍𝚡|Cθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,|𝚒𝚍𝚡|),if impure and ​λ​𝖾𝖿𝗌>|𝚒𝚍𝚡|\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}({\tt idx},r)=\begin{cases}C_{\theta}({\tt idx},\mathsf{efs}),&\text{if }{\tt idx}\text{ is pure w.r.t.\ }r\\ C_{\theta}({\tt idx},\lceil\lambda\mathsf{efs}\rceil),&\text{if impure and }\lambda\mathsf{efs}\leq|{\tt idx}|\\ C_{\theta}({\tt idx},|{\tt idx}|),&\text{if impure and }\lambda\mathsf{efs}>|{\tt idx}|\\ \end{cases}

The first case is a pure index that needs no post-filtering. The second inflates the priority queue to absorb unauthorized vectors. The third arises when inflation exceeds the index size and degenerates to a full scan. On real hardware each expansion is dominated by work that is constant in 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs}. It evaluates distances MM times using 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) floating-point operations each and fetches the corresponding neighbor vectors from memory, typically through cache misses. Thus, we uses the linear form Cθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,𝖾𝖿𝗌)C_{\theta}({\tt idx},\mathsf{efs}) to model the latency instead of the asymptotic bound in §2.1.

The marginal cost of one extra unit of 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} is therefore effectively constant, and measured latency is fit better by the linear form (e.g., R2=0.99R^{2}{=}0.99 vs. 0.980.98 for 𝖾𝖿𝗌​log⁡𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs}\log\mathsf{efs} when d=128d{=}128, M=16M{=}16; see Appendix B for details). We accordingly adopt Cθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,𝖾𝖿𝗌)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+b​𝖾𝖿𝗌+cC_{\theta}({\tt idx},\mathsf{efs})=a\log|{\tt idx}|+b\,\mathsf{efs}+c, with θ=(a,b,c)\theta=(a,b,c) calibrated once per deployment so that the coefficients absorb the effects of dd, MM, and the memory hierarchy. Appendix B gives the detailed derivation and how we estimate aa, bb, and cc. We now compare four partitioning strategies on a toy dataset of 10,00010{,}000 vectors with three roles {r1,r2,r3}\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\} (Figure 1).

∙\bullet Baseline 1 (Global Index). One index over the entire dataset; every query post-filters unauthorized results (SA = 1).

∙\bullet Baseline 2 (Oracle Index). An ideal query-predicate-aware HNSW baseline: for each role rr, construct an index over exactly 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r), the vectors authorized for rr. This oracle partition requires no post-filtering or search-scope expansion, but it duplicates every vector that is visible to multiple roles (SA = 1.5).

∙\bullet Strategy 3 (Merge). Exclusive blocks that are co-accessed are merged into shared groups. In Figure 1 the blocks of {r1}\{r_{1}\} and {r1,r2}\{r_{1},r_{2}\} are merged, as are those of {r1,r3}\{r_{1},r_{3}\} and {r1,r2,r3}\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}. No data is duplicated (SA = 1).

∙\bullet Strategy 4 (Copy). Selected blocks are duplicated so they co-locate with other blocks accessible to the same role. In Figure 1, the block {r1,r2}\{r_{1},r_{2}\} is copied into the group {r1}\{r_{1}\}. Queries with r2r_{2} access the original node {r1,r2}\{r_{1},r_{2}\}, eliminating impurity when searching for role r2r_{2} on the new data group. Similarly, the block {r1,r2,r3}\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\} is copied into the group {r1,r3}\{r_{1},r_{3}\} (SA = 1.2).

These four strategies span the storage–efficiency spectrum. Baseline 1 attains optimal storage (SA=1\textsf{SA}=1) but the highest query cost, since every query searches all data and then filters. Baseline 2 attains the oracle query cost but duplicates shared data (SA=1.5\textsf{SA}=1.5). Strategy 3 avoids duplication (SA=1\textsf{SA}=1); r1r_{1} and r3r_{3} hit pure indices while r2r_{2} still post-filters. Strategy 4 duplicates selectively (SA=1.2\textsf{SA}=1.2) to cut impurity, trading modest storage for lower latency.

2.3. Challenges

The four strategies expose a tension between SA and QA: improving one degrades the other. Selective merging (Strategy 3) and copying (Strategy 4) sit between the extremes and show that the tension can be eased by managing data blocks that are retrieved together. Copying is preferable to merging when storage permits, since it preserves the source block and avoids degrading other roles through impurity. These observations motivate an indexing scheme that combines copy and merge under a storage budget while ensuring high recall. Three challenges follow.

∙\bullet Data Partition. Given a user-specified SA budget, how should the dataset be partitioned to minimize QA while preserving recall? And since linear scan beats HNSW on small groups (Figure 2), how should HNSW indexing and linear scan be combined across groups of different sizes?

∙\bullet Index Selection. Given the indices built over those groups, which subset should a role query to retrieve its top-kk results efficiently?

∙\bullet Query Answering. How can search be coordinated across multiple indices, including impure ones that mix authorized and unauthorized vectors, such that redundant exploration is avoided and recall is preserved?

3. Data Partition and Index Selection

This section formalizes Data Partition and Index Selection and illustrates both on the dataset of Figure 1.

3.1. Problem Definition

Given a vector dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} and a SA budget, in which each vector is accessible to one or more roles, we seek a partition of 𝒟\mathcal{D} into groups suitable for indexing. The objective is threefold: (i) minimize the average estimated query cost; (ii) limiting the impurity of any group with respect to the roles that query it; and (iii) respect the given SA budget. We assume uniform single-role queries by default and extend to other workloads in §7. We assume that 𝒟\mathcal{D} and ℛ\mathcal{R} are static during construction, and discuss extensions to insertions, deletions, and permission changes in Appendix I.

Roles and Access Tags. Let ℛ={r1,r2,…}\mathcal{R}=\{r_{1},r_{2},\dots\} be the set of roles. Each vector in 𝒟\mathcal{D} carries a role combination τ⊆ℛ\tau\subseteq\mathcal{R} with |τ|≥1|\tau|\geq 1 that names the roles authorized to read it. For each τ\tau, the exclusive block N𝑒𝑥​(τ)N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau) is the set of vectors that are exclusively accessible to role set τ\tau. The dataset thus decomposes into a set of disjoint exclusive blocks, denoted as 𝒩𝑒𝑥\mathcal{N}_{\mathit{ex}}: 𝒩𝑒𝑥={N𝑒𝑥​(τ):τ⊆ℛ​and​|N𝑒𝑥​(τ)|>0}\mathcal{N}_{\mathit{ex}}=\{N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau):\tau\subseteq\mathcal{R}~\text{and}~|N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau)|>0\}. Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the set of role combinations with non-empty exclusive blocks, for example, 𝒯={{r1},{r2},{r3},{r1,r2},\mathcal{T}=\{\{r_{1}\},\{r_{2}\},\{r_{3}\},\{r_{1},r_{2}\}, {r1,r3},{r2,r3},{r1,r2,r3}}\{r_{1},r_{3}\},\{r_{2},r_{3}\},\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}\} in Figure 1. Let 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r) be all vectors accessible to rr, i.e., 𝒟(r)=⋃τ∈𝒯:r∈τN𝑒𝑥(τ)\mathcal{D}(r)=\bigcup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}:r\in\tau}N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau).

Index Set. An index is built over the union of one or more exclusive blocks, and two indices may share exclusive blocks. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} denote the set of all HNSW indices built over 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and let 𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}({\tt idx}) be the vectors used to build 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx}. Each index is then a union of exclusive blocks, i.e., 𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)=⋃τ′∈𝒯′N𝑒𝑥​(τ′)\mathcal{D}({\tt idx})=\bigcup_{\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{\prime}}N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau^{\prime}) for some 𝒯′⊆𝒯\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{T}, and the same block may appear in several indices. Let ℐ⁡(r)⊆ℐ\mathcal{I}(r)\subseteq\mathcal{I} be the indices used to answer queries for role rr. An index set ℐ\mathcal{I} is correct if, for every r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, ℐ⁡(r)\mathcal{I}(r) covers all of rr’s data: 𝒟⁡(r)⊆⋃𝚒𝚍𝚡∈ℐ⁡(r)𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}(r)\subseteq\bigcup_{{\tt idx}\in\mathcal{I}(r)}\mathcal{D}({\tt idx}), where 𝒟⁡(r)=⋃τ∈{τ∈𝒯∣r∈τ}N𝑒𝑥​(τ)\mathcal{D}(r)=\bigcup_{\tau\in\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}\mid r\in\tau\}}N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau).

Query Model. A query q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) is issued by a user with role rr and retrieves the top-kk nearest neighbors of 𝐱\mathbf{x} within 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r). The query may touch any subset ℐ⁡(r)⊆ℐ\mathcal{I}(r)\subseteq\mathcal{I} whose union covers 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r). The expected cost for role rr is the sum over its plan: Cost​(r)=∑𝚒𝚍𝚡∈ℐ⁡(r)CostH​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,r)\textsf{Cost}(r)=\sum_{{\tt idx}\in\mathcal{I}(r)}\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}({\tt idx},r).

Objective. Let Q={q1,q2,…}Q=\{q_{1},q_{2},\ldots\} be a uniform single-role workload in which each q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) draws r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} with equal probability. The estimated average query cost is

(2) AvgCost​(Q,ℐ)=1|Q|​∑q∈QCost​(r).\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I})=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\textsf{Cost}(r).
Definition 3.1.

Given a role-based dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, a workload QQ, and an SA budget β\beta, the Index Selection problem constructs an index set ℐ\mathcal{I} over 𝒟\mathcal{D} via merge and copy operations that minimizes AvgCost​(Q,ℐ)\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I}) subject to SA​(ℐ)≤β\textsf{SA}(\mathcal{I})\leq\beta.

The problem generalizes budgeted set cover: each candidate index covers a subset of ⋃rℒ𝑒𝑥​[r]\bigcup_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}[r] at a storage cost, and we must cover every role’s blocks under a knapsack constraint while minimizing a sub-additive query cost. Budgeted set cover is NP-hard (Khuller et al., 1999), so we do not seek exact solutions; §4–§5 give greedy heuristics, and Appendix §C gives the MILP used to bound their gap on small instances. We also note that although |𝒯|≤2|ℛ||\mathcal{T}|\leq 2^{|\mathcal{R}|} in the worst case, in practice |𝒯||\mathcal{T}| is bounded by the number of distinct permission sets the policy actually assigns, e.g.,641641–757757 on our benchmarks (Table 2).

3.2. Exclusive Lattices

The subset-containment relations among role combinations give the exclusive blocks a natural partial order. We organize them in an exclusive lattice and then optimize that lattice to form indexable data groups (§4 and §5).

Consider Strategy 4 in Figure 1. Each exclusive block is placed on a layer according to the cardinality of the role combination; with three roles, the lattice has at most three layers. Edges encode parent–child relations; upper-layer nodes are parents and lower-layer nodes are children. The block with role set {r2,r3}\{r_{2},r_{3}\}, for instance, is a child of both {r2}\{r_{2}\} and {r3}\{r_{3}\}. Edges thus mirror the containment hierarchy of the access-control policy.

Formally, the exclusive lattice is a directed acyclic graph ℒ𝑒𝑥=(𝒩𝑒𝑥,E)\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}=(\mathcal{N}_{\mathit{ex}},E). Each node N𝑒𝑥​(τ)∈𝒩𝑒𝑥N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau)\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathit{ex}} holds the data authorized for exactly τ\tau (§3), and EE captures how access scope widens from stricter to broader role sets. Nodes with the same |τ||\tau| share a layer; empty nodes and empty layers are omitted. Higher layers correspond to stricter access (fewer roles) and lower layers to broader access. An edge (N𝑒𝑥​(τ),N𝑒𝑥​(τ′))∈E(N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau),N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau^{\prime}))\in E links a parent to a child when both conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    Containment: τ⊆τ′\tau\subseteq\tau^{\prime}, so every role authorized at the parent is also authorized at the child.

  2. (2)

    Adjacency: |τ|<|τ′||\tau|<|\tau^{\prime}|, and no intermediate node N𝑒𝑥​(τ′′)N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau^{\prime\prime}) exists with |τ|<|τ′′|<|τ′||\tau|<|\tau^{\prime\prime}|<|\tau^{\prime}| and τ⊆τ′′⊆τ′\tau\subseteq\tau^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\tau^{\prime}.

A parent therefore has the more restrictive access set, and directed paths in ℒ𝑒𝑥\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}} define child–ancestor relations. Any role attached to an ancestor can read that ancestor and all of its descendants; a role introduced only at a descendant might not read the ancestor’s stricter block.

The data-partition problem can be cast as an optimization problem with nonlinear objective and constraints, but its size grows exponentially with the input. Appendix §C gives a non-convex linear-program formulation and its MILP simplification; the next two sections develop adaptive solutions instead.

4. Veda: The Adaptive Solution

Veda transforms the exclusive lattice ℒ𝑒𝑥=(𝒩𝑒𝑥,E)\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}=(\mathcal{N}_{\mathit{ex}},E) into an optimized lattice ℒ\mathcal{L} by applying copy and merge operations. The resulting lattice groups data that is queried together. Nodes with at least Λ\Lambda vectors receive HNSW indices; smaller nodes are kept as leftover vectors for linear scan.

Operations on Child–Ancestor Pairs. Veda acts only on child–ancestor pairs (Nc​(τ),Na​(τ′))(N_{c}(\tau),\,N_{a}(\tau^{\prime})) along paths in ℒ\mathcal{L}, where τ′⊆τ\tau^{\prime}\subseteq\tau. Every role that can read the ancestor Na​(τ′)N_{a}(\tau^{\prime}) can also read the child Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau), so any query that reaches the ancestor must also reach the child. Co-locating their data lets such queries be served from a single node. Two operations are defined on a pair (Nc​(τ),Na​(τ′))(N_{c}(\tau),\,N_{a}(\tau^{\prime})):

∙\bullet Copy: duplicate the exclusive data of Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) into Na​(τ′)N_{a}(\tau^{\prime}) and keep Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) as a separate node.

∙\bullet Merge: union Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) into Na​(τ′)N_{a}(\tau^{\prime}) and remove Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) from ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Each operation has a distinct trade-off. Copying preserves the source node but duplicates data, increasing SA. Merging avoids duplication but introduces impurity: roles that previously read a pure node may now encounter unauthorized vectors. In Strategy 3 of Figure 1, merging the node of {r1,r2}\{r_{1},r_{2}\} into the node of {r1}\{r_{1}\} forces r2r_{2}’s queries to traverse 10,00010{,}000 vectors exclusive to r1r_{1}. To navigate this trade-off, Veda takes a user-specified SA budget β\beta and ranks candidate operations with a benefit function: query-cost reduction per unit of added storage.

Definition 4.1 (Benefit Function).

Let Q={q1,q2,…}Q=\{q_{1},q_{2},\ldots\} be a uniform single-role query workload, where each q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) targets data accessible to r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}. For an operation ee on a child–ancestor pair (Nc​(τ),Na​(τ′))(N_{c}(\tau),\,N_{a}(\tau^{\prime})), let ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} be the lattice before and after ee, and let ℐ⁡(ℒ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{L}) denote the set of indices represented by lattice ℒ\mathcal{L}. The benefit of ee is

(3) f⁡(ℒ,e)=AvgCost​(Q,ℐ⁡(ℒ))−AvgCost​(Q,ℐ⁡(ℒ′))Δ​S​(e)+1,f(\mathcal{L},e)=\frac{\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{L}))-\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}))}{\Delta S(e)+1},

where AvgCost​(∗)\textsf{AvgCost}(*) is defined in Eq. 2, and Δ​S​(e)\Delta S(e) is the additional storage consumed by ee.

The numerator is the per-query reduction in average cost; the denominator normalizes by added storage. Adding 11 guards against division by zero, since merges consume no additional storage, and copies may also have Δ​S​(e)=0\Delta S(e)=0 after earlier operations make nodes impure. Although Veda starts from the exclusive lattice, an ancestor may already contain the child’s vectors because of prior copy or merge operations. A positive benefit means the operation reduces cost; a negative benefit signals degradation. Because copying preserves source nodes and never harms an existing query plan, Veda applies copy operations first within the budget β\beta (Theorem D.1, Appendix D).

Algorithm Overview. Algorithm 1 summarizes Veda. Starting from ℒ𝑒𝑥\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}, Veda enumerates the child–ancestor pairs 𝒞​𝒜​s\mathcal{CA}s represented by the lattice edges/paths, builds a query plan QP per role (i.e., which nodes to access to cover all data for each role, detailed in§6.1 later), and refines the lattice in three phases until the SA budget β\beta is exhausted or no beneficial operation remains, e.g., every remaining copy or merge candidate has non-positive benefit under Eq. 3.

  1. (1)

    Phase 1: Copy (§4.1). Greedily apply the highest-benefit copies, grouping related data while respecting β\beta.

  2. (2)

    Phase 2: Merge (§4.2). Merge residual small nodes into indexable groups (size ≥Λ\geq\Lambda), reclaiming any storage freed where prior copies overlap.

  3. (3)

    Phase 3: Finalize (Appendix §E.3). Decompose remaining unindexable groups into exclusive blocks for linear scan. If decomposition frees storage by removing duplicates, spend the reclaimed budget on materializing the pure part of any node that is highly impure for some role (Algorithm 11 in Appendix §E.3).

After Phase 3, each node in ℒ\mathcal{L} is a group of exclusive blocks. Veda builds an HNSW index for every node of size ≥Λ\geq\Lambda and keeps smaller nodes as leftover vectors for efficient linear scan.

4.1. Phase 1: Copying

The copy phase greedily selects and applies the most beneficial copies. A candidate e⁡(Nc​(τ),Na​(τ′))e(N_{c}(\tau),N_{a}(\tau^{\prime})) duplicates the vectors of Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) into Na​(τ′)N_{a}(\tau^{\prime}), consuming

Δ​S​(e)=|ℒ𝑒𝑥​[Nc​(τ)]|+|ℒ⁡[Na​(τ′)]|−|ℒ𝑒𝑥​[Nc​(τ)]∪ℒ⁡[Na​(τ′)]|.\Delta S(e)=|\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}[N_{c}(\tau)]|+|\mathcal{L}[N_{a}(\tau^{\prime})]|-|\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}[N_{c}(\tau)]\cup\mathcal{L}[N_{a}(\tau^{\prime})]|.

Greedy Selection.

Algorithm 2 gives the procedure. The available buffer is 𝑏𝑢𝑓=β​|ℒ𝑒𝑥|−|ℒ|\mathit{buf}=\beta|\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}|-|\mathcal{L}|. Here |ℒ||\mathcal{L}| is the total number of stored vectors across all nodes, counting duplicates. Let PR be the set of candidate copy operations e⁡(Nc,Na)e(N_{c},N_{a}) such that (Nc,Na)∈𝒞​𝒜​s(N_{c},N_{a})\in\mathcal{CA}s and both nodes are still present in the current lattice ℒ\mathcal{L}. The algorithm evaluates each candidate’s benefit f⁡(ℒ,e)f(\mathcal{L},e). At each step, it chooses the highest-benefit candidate e∗e^{*} and applies it only if the benefit is nonnegative and the copy fits the remaining budget:

(4) e∗=argmaxe∈PRf(ℒ,e),f(ℒ,e∗)≥0andΔS(e∗)≤𝑏𝑢𝑓.e^{*}=\arg\max_{e\in\textsf{PR}}f(\mathcal{L},e),\quad f(\mathcal{L},e^{*})\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\Delta S(e^{*})\leq\mathit{buf}.

Zero-benefit copies with f⁡(ℒ,e)=0f(\mathcal{L},e)=0 are admitted. Such a copy may not change the current query plan by itself, but after complementary descendants are copied into the same ancestor, QP may replace several child accesses with one ancestor access. After each copy, Veda updates the buffer, the query plan QP, and the candidate set PR, recomputing benefits only for pairs that involve the modified ancestor.

Theorem 4.2 (Correctness of Greedy Copy Phase).

Let ℒt\mathcal{L}_{t} be the lattice after tt greedy copy operations. Then:

  1. (1)

    Monotonicity: AvgCost​(Q,ℐ⁡(ℒt))≤AvgCost​(Q,ℐ⁡(ℒt−1))\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{L}_{t}))\leq\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{L}_{t-1})).

  2. (2)

    Budget Safety: |ℒt||ℒ𝑒𝑥|≤β\tfrac{|\mathcal{L}_{t}|}{|\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}|}\leq\beta.

  3. (3)

    Termination: the phase halts when no ee satisfies Equation 4.

Complexity. There are 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|2)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{2}) candidate pairs, and each benefit evaluation costs 𝒪⁡(|Q|⋅|𝒩|)\mathcal{O}(|Q|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|) to update the affected query costs. Each copy may trigger re-evaluation of up to 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|2)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{2}) pairs, and at most 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|) copies occur, giving a worst-case time of 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|5​|Q|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{5}|Q|).

4.2. Phase 2: Merge

Copying alone may leave too few indexable nodes. Copying is limited by the storage budget and preserves each copied child as a separate node. Thus, data may reside in nodes with fewer than Λ\Lambda vectors, leaving few groups large enough to index. Merging consolidates child nodes into their ancestors and can push more groups past the Λ\Lambda threshold without using storage. Unlike copying, merging is double-edged. It helps roles whose data is distributed across nodes into fewer, larger groups but hurts roles that now meet unauthorized vectors in the merged node. In Strategy 3 of Figure 1, merging the node of {r1,r2}\{r_{1},r_{2}\} into the node of {r1}\{r_{1}\} helps r1r_{1} (one fewer index to search) but hurts r2r_{2}, which must now traverse 10,00010{,}000 unauthorized vectors. Veda therefore applies a merge only when its benefit (Equation 3) is strictly positive.

Algorithm 3 applies merging operations greedily until no child–ancestor pair has positive benefit. Each step merges the highest-benefit child–ancestor pair, removes the child node, updates QP, and recomputes benefits only for pairs involving the modified ancestor.

Theorem 4.3 (Correctness of Merge Phase).

Let ℒt\mathcal{L}_{t} be the lattice after tt merge operations. Then:

  1. (1)

    Strict Improvement: AvgCost​(Q,ℐ⁡(ℒt))<AvgCost​(Q,ℐ⁡(ℒt−1))\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{L}_{t}))<\textsf{AvgCost}(Q,\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{L}_{t-1})).

  2. (2)

    Storage Reduction: if Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) and Na​(τ′)N_{a}(\tau^{\prime}) share exclusive blocks (from prior copies), then |ℒt|<|ℒt−1||\mathcal{L}_{t}|<|\mathcal{L}_{t-1}|.

  3. (3)

    Termination: the phase halts when no merge has positive benefit.

Complexity. Each merge removes one node, so at most 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|) merges occur. Each step re-evaluates 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|2)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{2}) candidate pairs at 𝒪⁡(|Q|⋅|𝒩|)\mathcal{O}(|Q|\!\cdot\!|\mathcal{N}|) per pair, for an overall 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|4​|Q|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{4}|Q|).

5. EffVeda: An Efficient Solution

EffVeda improves on Veda by giving the copy and merge phases narrower goals and a fixed traversal order. The copy phase traverses the exclusive lattice ℒ𝑒𝑥\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}} bottom-up and, in a single operation, duplicates a child node’s entire contents (not just its exclusive block) into one or more ancestors while keeping every node pure towards its original role set. This spends the SA budget only on disjoint ancestors, and a role’s query does not retrieve duplicate copies of the same vectors from multiple selected nodes. The merge phase then targets indexability: it greedily grows nodes that sit just below the threshold Λ\Lambda until they become indexable, without consuming storage.

EffVeda estimates benefit from the marginal cost reduction per role alone. Unlike Veda, it does not maintain a query plan QP to indicate which nodes to access for each role during construction. It also does not re-score child–ancestor candidates after each step. The two phases run once each, with no alternation and no post-processing copy pass.

5.1. Phase 1: Copying

EffVeda applies purity-preserving copying by processing ℒ\mathcal{L} in a bottom-up manner. At layer ℓ\ell, each node is copied into a set of disjoint partitioned ancestors so that every query formerly served by the node is now served by one of those ancestors. All nodes on yet-unprocessed upper layers stay pure for their original role sets. The source node is then redundant and can be removed from ℒ\mathcal{L}. We formalize the purity-preserving copy with valid partitions.

Valid Partitions. A valid partition of a child node Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) is a subset of its ancestors whose role sets fully cover τ\tau disjointly. As an example, in the lattice of Figure 3, N⁡({r1,r2})N(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}) and N⁡({r3})N(\{r_{3}\}) is a valid partition of N⁡({r1,r2,r3})N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}).

Definition 5.1 (Valid Partition of a Child Node).

Let Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) be a child node with ancestor set AcA_{c}. A subset Pc={Na​(τ1),Na​(τ2),…}⊆Ac\textsf{P}_{c}=\{N_{a}(\tau_{1}),N_{a}(\tau_{2}),\ldots\}\subseteq A_{c} is a valid partition of Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) if

  1. (1)

    Full coverage: τ=⋃Na​(τj)∈Pcτj\tau=\bigcup_{N_{a}(\tau_{j})\in\textsf{P}_{c}}\tau_{j}.

  2. (2)

    Disjoint roles: for all Na​(τj)N_{a}(\tau_{j}) and Na​(τj′)N_{a}(\tau_{j^{\prime}}) in Pc\textsf{P}_{c} (j≠j′j\neq j^{\prime}), τj∩τj′=∅\tau_{j}\cap\tau_{j^{\prime}}=\emptyset, hence ∑Na​(τj)∈Pc|τj|=|τ|\sum_{N_{a}(\tau_{j})\in\textsf{P}_{c}}|\tau_{j}|=|\tau|.

The child Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) is copied into each node in Pc\textsf{P}_{c}. Each ancestor stores only data authorized for its original roles, and every query that previously reached Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) is now answered through one of the ancestors in Pc\textsf{P}_{c}; correctness and purity are both preserved. In Figure 3, N⁡({r1,r2,r3})N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}) is copied into N⁡({r1,r2})N(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}) and N⁡({r3})N(\{r_{3}\}). Queries for r1r_{1} or r2r_{2} then go to N⁡({r1,r2})N(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}), queries for r3r_{3} go to N⁡({r3})N(\{r_{3}\}), and N⁡({r1,r2,r3})N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}) is never queried and can be deleted.

Theorem 5.2 (Node Purity after Copying).

Each ancestor Na​(τj)∈PcN_{a}(\tau_{j})\in\textsf{P}_{c} remains pure with respect to τj\tau_{j} after copying data from Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) into it, and must be visited by any query for roles in τj\tau_{j}.

Proof.

Since τj⊂τ\tau_{j}\subset\tau, any query for r∈τjr\in\tau_{j} also requires Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau), whose data now resides in Na​(τj)N_{a}(\tau_{j}). Roles τ∖τj\tau\setminus\tau_{j} are covered by disjoint ancestors Na​(τj′)∈PcN_{a}(\tau_{j^{\prime}})\in\textsf{P}_{c}, so purity holds for every role. ∎

Selecting a Valid Partition. A node Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) may admit many valid partitions. EffVeda scores each one and picks the best. Because every ancestor in a valid partition Pc\textsf{P}_{c} stays pure, the benefit can be computed directly without recomputing QP.

For a child Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) and disjoint ancestors Pc⊆Ac\textsf{P}_{c}\subseteq A_{c} that jointly cover τ\tau,

(5) f⁡(Nc​(τ),Pc)=∑Na​(τj)∈Pc∑r∈τjΔc​(Nc​(τ),Na​(τj),r)|ℒ⁡[Nc​(τ)]|⋅(|Pc|−1),f(N_{c}(\tau),\textsf{P}_{c})=\frac{\sum_{N_{a}(\tau_{j})\in\textsf{P}_{c}}\sum_{r\in\tau_{j}}\Delta_{c}(N_{c}(\tau),N_{a}(\tau_{j}),r)}{|\mathcal{L}[N_{c}(\tau)]|\cdot(|\textsf{P}_{c}|-1)},

where, under uniform role access,

Δc​(Nc​(τ),Na​(τj),r)\displaystyle\Delta_{c}(N_{c}(\tau),N_{a}(\tau_{j}),r) =CostH​(IH​(Nc​(τ)),r)+CostH​(IH​(Na​(τj)),r)\displaystyle=\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}\!\left(I^{\textsf{H}}(N_{c}(\tau)),r\right)+\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}\!\left(I^{\textsf{H}}(N_{a}(\tau_{j})),r\right)

|Pc|−1|\textsf{P}_{c}|-1 additional copies of Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) are created, each with the storage overhead of |ℒ​[Nc​(τ)]||\mathcal{L}[N_{c}(\tau)]|. For each ancestor Na​(τj)∈PcN_{a}(\tau_{j})\in\textsf{P}_{c}, the gain for each role in τj\tau_{j} is the same, thus Eq. 5 can be simplified to:

(6) f⁡(Nc​(τ),Pc)=∑Na​(τj)∈Pc|τj|⋅Δc​(Nc​(τ),Na​(τj),r)|ℒ⁡[Nc​(τ)]|⋅(|Pc|−1).f(N_{c}(\tau),\textsf{P}_{c})=\frac{\sum_{N_{a}(\tau_{j})\in\textsf{P}_{c}}|\tau_{j}|\cdot\Delta_{c}(N_{c}(\tau),N_{a}(\tau_{j}),r)}{|\mathcal{L}[N_{c}(\tau)]|\cdot(|\textsf{P}_{c}|-1)}.
Lemma 5.4.

For any valid partition Pc\textsf{P}_{c}, f⁡(Nc​(τ),Pc)>0f(N_{c}(\tau),\textsf{P}_{c})>0. Moreover, since every valid partition covers τ\tau exactly once, the role-weighted gain ∑j|τj|​Δc​(⋅)\sum_{j}|\tau_{j}|\,\Delta_{c}(\cdot) differs across partitions only through the ancestor sizes |Na​(τj)||N_{a}(\tau_{j})|, which enter Δc\Delta_{c} logarithmically; the denominator instead grows linearly in |Pc||\textsf{P}_{c}|. Smaller partitions therefore dominate. (Proof in Appendix F.2.)

EffVeda finds the best valid partition of a child given its ancestor set and a target size η\eta. In practice this search is cheap: EffVeda enumerates disjoint ancestor subsets in increasing η\eta (starting at 22), and small subsets usually suffice. Under heavy skew, however, valid partitions may need larger η\eta and the search space grows exponentially; in some cases no valid partition exists. If the lattice of Figure 3 held only N⁡({r1})N(\{r_{1}\}), N⁡({r1,r2})N(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}), N⁡({r2,r3})N(\{r_{2},r_{3}\}), and N⁡({r1,r2,r3})N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}), no valid partition would cover the bottom node.

Without loss of generality, EffVeda restricts the search to η=2\eta=2. Besides copying into two ancestors each time, EffVeda also admits a degenerate option: copy into a single ancestor and keep the source node. Both options add exactly one copy of the child, so their storage overheads match. For each ancestor Na​(τ′)∈AcN_{a}(\tau^{\prime})\in A_{c}, EffVeda scores copying Nc​(τ)N_{c}(\tau) into Na​(τ′)N_{a}(\tau^{\prime}) and identifies the complementary ancestor with role set τ∖τ′\tau\setminus\tau^{\prime}. If that complementary ancestor also lies in AcA_{c} (a valid partition of size two), EffVeda scores the two-ancestor copy as well. After evaluating all single-ancestor copies and all valid two-ancestor partitions induced by ancestors in AcA_{c}, EffVeda chooses the candidate with the highest copy benefit. Algorithm 5 summarizes the procedure; Appendix F.1 extends it to larger partitions. The complexity drops to 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|2)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{2}). The algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 13 in Appendix §F.2.

Although EffVeda uses a different formula in Equation 3 for computing benefits of copy operations, the two are equivalent. Take the lattice in Figure 3 and copy N⁡({r1,r2,r3})N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}) into both N⁡({r1,r2})N(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}) and N⁡({r3})N(\{r_{3}\}). Before the copy, queries for r3r_{3} must visit N⁡({r3})N(\{r_{3}\}), N⁡({r1,r3})N(\{r_{1},r_{3}\}), N⁡({r2,r3})N(\{r_{2},r_{3}\}), and N⁡({r1,r2,r3})N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\}) separately; afterward they visit three nodes. The gain for querying r3r_{3} is CostH​(IH​(N⁡({r3})),r3)\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}(I^{\textsf{H}}(N(\{r_{3}\})),r_{3}) ++ CostH​(IH​(N⁡({r1,r2,r3})),r3)\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}(I^{\textsf{H}}(N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\})),r_{3}) −- CostH​(IH​(N⁡({r3})∪N⁡({r1,r2,r3})),r3)\textsf{Cost}_{\textsf{H}}(I^{\textsf{H}}(N(\{r_{3}\})\cup N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\})),r_{3}). The same computation applies to r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}. Summing the two gains and dividing by the storage overhead |ℒ⁡[N⁡({r1,r2,r3})]||\mathcal{L}[N(\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\})]| yields the operation’s benefit.

5.2. Phase 2: Merging

The merge phase processes nodes in descending size order and prioritizes those just below the indexing threshold Λ\Lambda, combining them into indexable nodes to improve query efficiency without adding storage. We note that all nodes are pure towards their original role sets after Phase 1. A merge may pair a node N⁡(τ)N(\tau) with one of its “relative” nodes, including an ancestor Na​(τ′)N_{a}(\tau^{\prime}), a descendant, or a sibling, provided the benefit is positive. As all nodes N⁡(τ)∈ℒN(\tau)\in\mathcal{L} are pure towards their role sets τ\tau, queries for any role r∉τr\notin\tau continue to route elsewhere, so correctness is preserved. As in Veda’s Phase 2, merging in EffVeda adds no storage but may introduce impurity.

Evaluating Merge Benefit. The merge score estimates the cost saved by replacing two node visits with one merged-node visit. The key invariant from Phase 1 is that every surviving node N⁡(τ)∈ℒN(\tau)\in\mathcal{L} is still pure with respect to its original role set τ\tau. Even if it might mix data copied from child nodes with larger role sets, only queries for roles in τ\tau are routed to N⁡(τ)N(\tau) before the merge. Thus, when evaluating a candidate merge of Nx​(τx)N_{x}(\tau_{x}) and Ny​(τy)N_{y}(\tau_{y}), EffVeda treats the two inputs as pure nodes touched by τx\tau_{x} and τy\tau_{y}, respectively. Thus, the benefit of merge operations can be estimated using a similar formula to the copy benefit function Eq. 5. The difference is that the merge benefit function takes into account the impurity penalty for roles that are authorized for only part of the merged node. This score adds the role-wise costs of the two pure nodes before the merge and subtracts the role-wise cost of the combined node after the merge, including the impurity penalty for roles that are authorized for only part of the merged node. Since merging adds no storage, EffVeda applies only candidates with positive benefit.

Greedy Execution. Algorithm 6 processes nodes in descending size order and, for each node, selects the ancestor, descendant, or sibling with the highest positive merge benefit. Each node participates in at most one merge, which limits impurity from accumulating across repeated merge operations. If the relative Nr​(τ′)N_{r}(\tau^{\prime}) is a child of Ni​(τ)N_{i}(\tau), the merge proceeds upward; otherwise the ancestor merges into the relative. Once the merged node reaches Λ\Lambda, processing advances to the next node; otherwise merging continues until the node is indexable. This procedure grows small nodes into indexable ones while preserving the lattice structure and the global storage budget.

Choice of Veda and EffVeda. Veda explores the full child–ancestor candidate space and yields slightly lower QA (Exps 7.3 and 7.3) at 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|5​|Q|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{5}|Q|) construction cost; EffVeda reaches a comparable layout in 𝒪⁡(|𝒩|2)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{N}|^{2}) per phase. We recommend EffVeda when the number of distinct role combinations is large in the dataset or when policies change frequently enough that re-optimization (Appendix I) dominates, and Veda when the policy is small and static and the last few percent of QA matter.

6. Query Answering

This section describes how access-controlled top-kk queries are answered once the lattice has been optimized. As in §4, nodes with at least Λ\Lambda vectors receive HNSW indices, and each such index may span several exclusive blocks. Nodes below Λ\Lambda are decomposed into individual exclusive blocks N𝑒𝑥​(τ)N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau) and kept as leftovers for linear scan. Given a query q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r), two tasks remain: (i) select a minimal set of nodes whose union covers exactly the data authorized for rr (§6.1); and (ii) search the selected HNSW indices and leftovers while filtering unauthorized vectors out of impure indices (§6.2).

6.1. Query Plan Construction

Given the lattice ℒ\mathcal{L} produced by Veda or EffVeda, the query plan identifies, for each role r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, the nodes that together cover 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r). We write the plan as QP​(r)=(ℐ​(r),𝒰​(r))\textsf{QP}(r)=(\mathcal{I}(r),\mathcal{U}(r)), where ℐ⁡(r)\mathcal{I}(r) is the set of HNSW indices searched for rr and 𝒰⁡(r)\mathcal{U}(r) is the set of leftover vectors scanned linearly. A plan is valid if it covers all authorized data for rr; among valid plans we prefer the one with minimum estimated cost, i.e., a minimal cover.

Blocks to Cover. Let ℒ𝑒𝑥​[r]={N𝑒𝑥​(τ)∈ℒ𝑒𝑥∣r∈τ}\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}[r]=\{N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau)\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}\mid r\in\tau\} be the exclusive blocks authorized for rr. Because of copy operations, each exclusive block may live in several nodes of the optimized lattice. Define the container map

Φ:ℒ𝑒𝑥→2ℒ,Φ⁡(N𝑒𝑥​(τ))={N⁡(τ′)∈ℒ∣N𝑒𝑥​(τ)⊆N⁡(τ′)}.\Phi:\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}}\to 2^{\mathcal{L}},\qquad\Phi(N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau))=\{N(\tau^{\prime})\in\mathcal{L}\mid N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau)\subseteq N(\tau^{\prime})\}.

Plan Construction. If an authorized exclusive block has only one container, that container is mandatory:

{N⁡(τ′)∈ℒ∣N⁡(τ′)∈Φ⁡(N𝑒𝑥​(τ))​and​|Φ⁡(N𝑒𝑥​(τ))|=1}⊆QP​(r).\{N(\tau^{\prime})\in\mathcal{L}\mid N(\tau^{\prime})\in\Phi(N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau))~\text{and}~|\Phi(N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau))|=1\}\subseteq\textsf{QP}(r).

With the mandatory nodes fixed, the remaining blocks are covered by choosing among their candidate containers. This residual cover can be solved exactly with an ILP or approximately with a greedy heuristic. Appendix §G gives both procedures (Algorithm 14 and Algorithm 15).

6.2. Coordinated Top-kk Query Execution

A plan QP​(r)\textsf{QP}(r) may mix pure indices, impure indices, and leftover vectors, as defined in §2.2, and execution depends on how each component relates to rr. Leftovers and pure indices can be searched directly. Impure indices need authorization filtering and may need inflated search parameters efs based on impurity to cover enough authorized candidates.

The simplest strategy searches each component independently: scan 𝒰⁡(r)\mathcal{U}(r), run standard HNSW top-kk on each pure index, run inflated HNSW search on each impure index, filter, and merge into a heap of size kk. For an impure index the inflation factor λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}} is computed as in Eq. 1, and the query uses k′=⌈λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r​k⌉k^{\prime}=\lceil\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}k\rceil with efs′=⌈λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r​efs⌉\textsf{efs}^{\prime}=\lceil\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}\textsf{efs}\rceil. Algorithm 16 in Appendix §G gives the procedure.

Consider the merged group in Strategy 3 of Figure 1 that builds one HNSW index 𝚒𝚍𝚡⁡({r1,r2}){\tt idx}(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}) over N𝑒𝑥​({r1})∪N𝑒𝑥​({r1,r2})N^{\mathit{ex}}(\{r_{1}\})\cup N^{\mathit{ex}}(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}). Both exclusive blocks contain 10,00010{,}000 vectors. For a query q=(𝐱,r2)q=(\mathbf{x},r_{2}), only the vectors in N𝑒𝑥​({r1,r2})N^{\mathit{ex}}(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}) are authorized inside this index, so λ𝚒𝚍𝚡⁡({r1,r2})r2=⌈20,000/10,000⌉=2\lambda^{r_{2}}_{{\tt idx}(\{r_{1},r_{2}\})}=\lceil 20{,}000/10{,}000\rceil=2. For a top-22 query, the baseline execution searches 𝚒𝚍𝚡⁡({r1,r2}){\tt idx}(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}) with k′=λ𝚒𝚍𝚡⁡({r1,r2})r2​k=4k^{\prime}=\lambda^{r_{2}}_{{\tt idx}(\{r_{1},r_{2}\})}k=4 and filters unauthorized results. Suppose the HNSW search returns [(u1,0.03),(v1,0.04),(u2,0.06),(v2,0.09)],[(u_{1},0.03),(v_{1},0.04),(u_{2},0.06),(v_{2},0.09)], where u1,u2∈N𝑒𝑥​({r1})u_{1},u_{2}\in N^{\mathit{ex}}(\{r_{1}\}) and v1,v2∈N𝑒𝑥​({r1,r2})v_{1},v_{2}\in N^{\mathit{ex}}(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}). The query filters out u1u_{1} and u2u_{2}, keeps v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}, and returns [(v1,0.04),(v2,0.09)][(v_{1},0.04),(v_{2},0.09)] as the top-22 authorized results from this component. If QP​(r2)\textsf{QP}(r_{2}) contains additional indices or leftover blocks, their authorized candidates are merged with these two candidates and the closest two overall are returned.

Independent inflated search wastes work when other components in the plan already supply strong authorized candidates. Coordinated search avoids this by querying pure sources first; the scheme is an instance of threshold-based top-kk aggregation (Fagin et al., 2001) adapted to graph-based ANN, where the global kk-th distance plays the role of Fagin’s threshold and each sub-index is a sorted-access source. Leftovers and pure indices contain only authorized data for rr, so their results initialize a global heap 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS} of size kk. Let vkgv_{k}^{g} be the current kk-th entry in 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS}; its distance dist​(𝐱,vkg)\textsf{dist}(\mathbf{x},v_{k}^{g}) is the global bound. For each impure index 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx}, coordinated search first runs an uninflated HNSW probe with efs, filters authorized candidates, and merges only those that improve 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS}. Let vklv_{k}^{l} be the kk-th entry of the unfiltered local result from the impure index𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx}. If dist​(𝐱,vkg)≤dist​(𝐱,vkl)\textsf{dist}(\mathbf{x},v_{k}^{g})\leq\textsf{dist}(\mathbf{x},v_{k}^{l}) then, under the HNSW search accuracy assumption, no unseen vector in 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} is likely to improve the global heap, and the search on 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} stops early. Otherwise the search resumes with 𝖾𝖿𝗌\mathsf{efs} inflated by λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}} and merges the newly found authorized candidates. Algorithm 7 gives the procedure; the resumed base-layer traversal under the global bound is detailed in Algorithm 17 (Appendix §G.2).

Figure 4 illustrates the procedure with one pure and one impure index. The leftover scan and the pure-index search first populate 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS} with authorized candidates. For the impure index, the kk-th unfiltered local candidate is compared to the global kk-th authorized result. If the local candidate is already farther, the rest of that index is unlikely to enter the global top-kk under the HNSW search accuracy assumption; otherwise the impure search expands with efs′\textsf{efs}^{\prime}. Appendix §G.3 formalizes the inflated-kk accuracy condition: if the inflated search reaches the position of the kk-th authorized vector in the unfiltered ranking, filtering returns the true authorized top-kk with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Independently of recall, every candidate is checked against the role’s authorization before admission to the result set 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS}, so the returned set is always a subset of 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r).

7. Evaluations

In this section we evaluate Veda and EffVeda against the global index, the oracle index, ACORN-1 (Patel et al., 2024), ACORN-γ\gamma, SIEVE (Li et al., 2025), and HoneyBee (Zhong et al., 2025). We study:

∙\bullet Index construction. End-to-end build time as the SA budget grows (Exp 7.2), the number of indexed data and leftover data (Exp 7.2), the number of HSNW indices built in total (Exp 7.2), and how tightly the achieved SA tracks the user-specified budget (Exp 7.2).

∙\bullet Impact of parameters. Robustness of the results to the indexing threshold Λ\Lambda (Exp 7.3), the contribution of coordinated search measured as phase-2 skip rate and efs savings on impure indices (Exp 7.3), and the impact of the HNSW search parameter efs (Exp 7.3).

∙\bullet End-to-end QPS vs. recall.

∙\bullet Query processing. QA under different values of SA (Exp 7.3), the purity of the data each method selects per query (Exp 7.3), QPS vs Recall@10 of the methods on SIFT-1M, PAPER, and AMZN (Exp 7.3), and impact of query sensitivity (Exp 7.3).

∙\bullet Workload variation. Weighted single-role queries (Exp 7.3), and multi-role queries whose authorized region can span most of 𝒟\mathcal{D}; the latter delineates where partitioning should yield to filtered search on a global index (Exp 7.3).

7.1. Setup

Setting. All experiments were conducted on a machine running macOS 26.3 (Darwin 25.3.0, ARM64) with an Apple M4 Max processor (14 cores) and 36 GiB of unified memory.

Datasets. We use SIFT-1M (Jegou et al., 2010), PAPER (Wang et al., 2022), and Amazon Books Reviews (AMZN) (He and McAuley, 2016; McAuley et al., 2015) (Table 2). Access-control policies are generated from OrgAccess (Sanyal et al., 2025), which grants each role the union of a set of departments. We use the Easy subset (roles clustered to a target count), and Medium/Hard unmodified. Block sizes follow a shifted Zipf distribution (i+s)−α(i+s)^{-\alpha}  (Zipf, 2016; Mandelbrot, 1953); the number of blocks assigned to department jj follows (j+s′)−α′(j+s^{\prime})^{-\alpha^{\prime}}. Higher skew in this permission distribution means that a few departments are associated with substantially more data than the rest.

Compared Methods. We compare Veda and EffVeda with two data partitioning methods: 1) SIEVE (Li et al., 2025) and 2) HoneyBee (Zhong et al., 2025). We also include in-search filtering methods 3) ACORN-1 (Patel et al., 2024) and 4) ACORN-γ\gamma (Patel et al., 2024), and two baselines: 5) Global Index (Baseline 1) and 6) Oracle Index (Baseline 2) when evaluating the throughputs of these methods. For all partition-based methods (SIEVE, HoneyBee, Veda, EffVeda) we apply SIEVE’s heterogeneous-search rule (Li et al., 2025) and downscale efs on each sub-index by the log-ratio of its size to |𝒟||\mathcal{D}|, so small partitions are not over-searched. As SIEVE relies on historical queries, it is given a held-out workload sampled from the same role distribution as the test queries.

Metrics. We report four metrics: 1) SA measures the storage overhead; 2) QA measures query cost normalized to oracle indexing, isolating algorithmic efficiency from hardware constants and quantifying how far a method deviates from Oracle; 3) QPS measures end-to-end query throughput; and 4) recall@kk measures the fraction of the true top-kk results (obtained by brute-force scan over 𝒟\mathcal{D}) that are present in the result sets.

Parameters. According to literature (Li et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025; Patel et al., 2024; Malkov and Yashunin, 2018), we set the HNSW parameter MM to 16, 32, and 32 for SIFT-1M, PAPER, and AMZN, respectively, and set the default values of the searching parameter efs and the HNSW construction parameter efc to 100 and 200, respectively. The construction parameter γ\gamma in ACORN-γ\gamma is set to 1/ms1/m_{s} (Patel et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025), where msm_{s} is the minimum selectivity, i.e., the smallest fraction of the dataset admitted by any role whose selectivity exceeds the brute-force bound. By default, we set γ\gamma to 1212 (Patel et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Following (Li et al., 2025), we impose a brute-force search bound of 1/121/12 for ACORN-1 and ACORN-γ\gamma. Without this bound, γ\gamma becomes prohibitively large (e.g., 23,81023{,}810 for SIFT-1M), causing each HNSW node to store up to 23,⋅M23{,}810\!\cdot\!M neighbors instead of MM, which is impractical. Based on the analysis in Figure 2, we set the indexability threshold Λ\Lambda to 2,900, 3,000, and 2,600 for SIFT-1M, PAPER, and AMZN, respectively. We further validate the robustness of Veda and EffVeda to the choice of Λ\Lambda in Exp 7.3 and Appendix H.1. For methods that require a desired SA, i.e., Veda, EffVeda, SIEVE, and HoneyBee, we set the desired SA to a small value, i.e., 1.1 by default, to highlight the advantages of data partitioning in vector search with access control. This setting demonstrates that even a modest storage overhead yield big performance gains. Additional evaluations under different values of SA are deferred to Appendix H.

Query workloads. A query is q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) for single-role queries or q=(𝐱,τ)q=(\mathbf{x},\tau) with τ⊆ℛ\tau\subseteq\mathcal{R} for multi-role queries. We use four workloads: (1) uniform single-role: each role drawn with probability 1/|ℛ|1/|\mathcal{R}|; (2) weighted single-role: role rr drawn with probability proportional to |𝒟⁡(r)||\mathcal{D}(r)|; (3) uniform multi-role: each role combination τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} (|τ|>1|\tau|>1) with non-empty exclusive block drawn uniformly; and (4) weighted multi-role: τ\tau drawn with probability proportional to the number of vectors exclusively accessible to τ\tau. For each workload, we create 100 queries, and run the 100 queries 10 times in evaluation. The final result is the average of the 10 runs. By default, we use SIFT-1M with uniform single-role queries. Exps 7.2–7.3 use single-role workloads, and Exp 7.3 evaluates with uniform multi-role queries and weighted multi-role queries. The query vector 𝐱\mathbf{x} may or may not be drawn from the queried roles’ own authorized data. We capture this with query sensitivity that controls how often the query vector comes from the queried role’s own data. For a single-role query q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r), a sensitivity of 1.01.0 means all query vectors are drawn from the 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r), while a sensitivity of 00 means all of the query vectors are drawn from 𝒟∖𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathcal{D}(r). By default, we set the sensitivity to 1.0.

7.2. Index Creation Evaluation

Exp 1. Index-creation time vs. SA. Figure 5(a) reports end-to-end build time (partitioning plus HNSW construction) and partitioning time as SA varies over 1.01.0, 1.11.1, 1.31.3, 1.51.5, 2.02.0, and 3.03.0. EffVeda is consistently faster than Veda because its bottom-up traversal in copying identifies candidate ancestors more efficiently and avoids re-scoring candidate pairs. HoneyBee spends substantially more time in data partitioning, whereas SIEVE has comparable partitioning time because it selects predicate subsets from the workload instead of reorganizing the data.

Exp 2. Number of Indexed vs. Leftover Data. Figure 5(b) reports the number of indexed data and leftover data for Veda and EffVeda. For both approaches, most data are indexed, and the total number of data grows with the SA budget.

Exp 3. Number of indices vs. SA. We vary SA over 1.01.0, 1.11.1, 1.31.3, 1.51.5, 2.02.0, and 3.03.0 and report the number of indices produced by the data partitioning approaches. Figure 5(c) shows Veda and EffVeda produce more indices than SIEVE and HoneyBee at every SA budget, as the exclusive lattice exposes fine-grained role-combination blocks, and a larger budget lets more of them be copied into indexable partitions. SIEVE creates data partitions based on historical query workloads, while HoneyBee uses coarser partitions and therefore produces the fewest indices.

Exp 4. Desired vs. achieved SA. We vary SA over 1.01.0, 1.11.1, 1.31.3, 1.51.5, 2.02.0, and 3.03.0 to evaluate how closely each data-partitioning method meets the requested SA. Figure 5(d) shows that Veda and EffVeda track the target SA tightly. HoneyBee and SIEVE account for storage consumption only before admitting a partition, so their final admission can overshoot the target.

7.3. Query-Based Evaluations

Exp 5. QA vs. SA. Figure 6(a) uses QA to measure how much each method deviates from Oracle, where lower QA is preferred. The results show that Veda and EffVeda outperform HoneyBee and SIEVE across the range. Most of the gain appears at small SA: a modest amount of extra storage removes a large share of unnecessary search work because the copy phase spends the budget on high-benefit duplicates, the merge phase turns small residual nodes into indexable groups, and finalization redirects queries away from highly impure nodes when pure materializations fit in the reclaimed budget. The Veda and EffVeda curves are not strictly monotone. Both algorithms optimize a discrete lattice under a hard storage budget, so different SA settings can leave different residual nodes for finalization. A higher SA budget may trigger copy or merge operations that changes which nodes cross the indexing threshold Λ\Lambda, or which highly impure nodes are finalized.

Exp 6. Purity of selected data. Figure 6(b) reports the fraction of data touched per query that is actually authorized for the queried role; higher purity means fewer wasted candidates are included in the indices queried. Veda and EffVeda achieve high purity across all SA budgets due to our efficient lattice construction strategies. SIEVE’s purity depends on efs (we plot efs==100 and 500). A larger beam (higher efs) pushes more queries to brute-force scan, resulting in higher purity. HoneyBee achieves the lowest purity across all SA budgets. Purity directly explains the QA ordering in Exp 7.3.

Exp 7. Number of indices per query. Table 3 reports the number of HNSW indices each query touches on average; fewer indices means less index-switching overhead. Veda usually queries fewer indices than EffVeda at tight SA budgets, because its construction strategy exhaustively considers candidate node pairs for merge and copy and can therefore concentrate the query plan into a smaller set of nodes. Overall, both methods touch fewer than seven indices per query on average, so index switching is not a dominant source of overhead.

Exp 8. Indexing threshold. Table 4 varies Λ\Lambda from 2,500 to 3,300 at SA=1.1=1.1 and reports the QPS of Veda and EffVeda. QPS changes mildly as Λ\Lambda varies; Veda stays near 2,040 and EffVeda near 1,700, peaking near Λ=2,900\Lambda=2{,}900. The results show that our methods are not sensitive to the exact indexing threshold. A lower Λ\Lambda produces more indexable nodes in the lattice, which trades scan cost for index-switching overhead; vice versa. The finalization stage resolves highly impure nodes effectively, further absorbing most differences in the outcome lattices of different Λ\Lambda. Results of SA=1.3,1.5=1.3,1.5 are in Appendix H.1.

Exp 9. Effect of coordinated search. Tables 5 and 6 isolate the contribution of coordinated search on impure-index visits. Phase 2 is skipped on at least 67.95%67.95\% of impure visits at every SA, resulting in the inflated efs cut by 8.57%8.57\%–23.09%23.09\%. Both Veda and EffVeda incorporate efficient finalization that handles highly impure nodes, thus the surviving impure indices have low impurity. Moreover, coordinated search leverages the tight bound of the global top-kk to suppress phase 2 entirely with high probability.

Exp 10. Effect of efs. Figure 6(c) reports QPS over efs varying as 10, 50, 100, 300, 500, 1000. QPS falls for all methods as efs grows because a larger beam explores more candidates in HNSW search. Baseline 1 (Global Index) is the slowest, while Baseline 2 (Oracle) is the upper bound. It searches a single pure index for each query and would not suffer from unauthorized candidates. Veda and EffVeda remain the strongest practical methods across the range. ACORN-1 is competitive at small efs. ACORN-γ\gamma is steadier and catches up with the partitioning methods at large efs. lower beams. HoneyBee remains much lower due to coarse, uncoordinated impure data partitions. Appendix H.2 shows results on PAPER and AMZN.

Exp 11. Comparison with other methods across datasets. We compare Veda and EffVeda with other methods using QPS and Recall@10 on SIFT-1M, PAPER, and AMZN. We vary efs over 10, 50, 100, 300, 500, and 1000, so each curve shows the trade-off: larger efs improves recall but lowers QPS. Figures 6(d), 7(a), and 7(b) show that Veda and EffVeda consistently occupy the upper-right frontier. They reach near-oracle recall while preserving high throughput because their partitions keep most searches on pure or low-impurity indices. SIEVE also reaches high recall, but its workload-driven partitions might leave more impure candidates, so it might have lower QPS than our approaches at matched recall. ACORN-1 achieves high QPS only at low recall. ACORN-γ\gamma is more accurate than ACORN-1 as the augmented graph helps recover authorized neighbors, but it still pays global-graph traversal cost. HoneyBee achieves lower QPS as it spend substantial work on unauthorized data.

Exp 12. Query sensitivity. Figure 7(c) reports Recall@10 over varying query sensitivity as 00, 0.250.25, 0.50.5, 0.750.75, and 1.01.0. Veda, EffVeda, SIEVE, and Oracle Index hold Recall@10 ≥0.99\geq 0.99 most of the time. ACORN-1 stays below 0.400.40, while ACORN-γ\gamma sits at 0.940.94–0.970.97, as filtering a global graph fail to recover all authorized data. Baseline 1 and HoneyBee degrade to 0.900.90–0.930.93. When the query lies outside 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r), the authorized neighbors are scattered and their search does not reach them.

Exp 13. Weighted single-role queries. Figure 7(d) compare the approaches with weighted single-role queries. Veda, EffVeda and SIEVE achieve competitive performance. Performance of ACORN-1, ACORN-γ\gamma, and HoneyBee are similar to Exp 7.3.

Exp 14. Multi-role queries. A multi-role query authorizes the union of several roles, so its region can cover most of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Pure partition execution then visits many sub-indices and merges many candidate lists. We therefore keep one additional global HNSW index and route a query to filtered global search whenever its authorized region exceeds 80%80\% of |𝒟||\mathcal{D}|; this adds exactly 11 to SA. Correspondingly, we set the desired SA to 2.1 for HoneyBee and SIEVE. Figures 8(a) and 8(b) show that with this fallback Veda and EffVeda stay close to SIEVE and Baseline 2 in the high-recall region on the uniform mixed-role workload and the weighted mixed-role workload. The experiment marks the crossover point argued in §1: partitioning wins for selective access, filtered global search wins for broad access.

8. Related Work

The problem of access-controlled vector search begins after the policy is fixed and asks how the retrieval layer should answer top-kk vector queries over the records visible to the querying role. This places Veda and EffVeda between general ANN indexing (Johnson et al., 2019; Malkov and Yashunin, 2018; Subramanya et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2020), filtered vector search (Gollapudi et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025), and RBAC-aware partitioning (Zhong et al., 2025). General ANN indices supply the building blocks but assume a single global search space; we therefore focus the remainder of this section on a qualitative comparison with the four systems closest to our setting, Filtered-DiskANN (Gollapudi et al., 2023), ACORN (Patel et al., 2024), SIEVE (Li et al., 2025), and HoneyBee (Zhong et al., 2025), and defer the full landscape of related works to Appendix J.

Predicate Model. Filtered-DiskANN and UNG (Cai et al., 2024) bake label predicates into graph construction, and ACORN traverses the predicate-induced subgraph of an HNSW index for arbitrary Boolean filters. All three treat the predicate as query-supplied metadata. SIEVE and HoneyBee instead exploit that the predicate distribution is known offline, SIEVE from a historical workload, HoneyBee from the RBAC role lattice, and materialize sub-indexes accordingly. Veda and EffVeda follows the latter view but represents the policy as exclusive role-subset blocks, so every role’s visible set is an exact union of blocks rather than an approximate match against a learned filter.

Storage–Latency Trade-off. Filtered-DiskANN and ACORN keep storage close to a single index (SA near 11) and pay at query time when the predicate is selective. SIEVE and HoneyBee expose an explicit memory budget and select sub-indexes (SIEVE) or partitions (HoneyBee) under it. Veda exposes the same knob but explores it with two primitives, including merge, which trades latency for storage by combining co-accessed blocks, and copy, which trades storage for latency by replicating a block into a co-accessed group.

Query Execution. ACORN and Filtered-DiskANN answer every query from one graph. SIEVE routes each query to the single cheapest subsuming sub-index (or brute force), and HoneyBee routes a role to the partition set implied by its split. None of them lets results from one index influence search on another. EffVeda instead runs a coordinated multi-index search: pure partitions are probed first and their top-kk distances tighten a global threshold that prunes the subsequent beam search on impure partitions and residual scans. This is the mechanism that lets Veda tolerate impure groups without inflating efs to the worst-case λ​efs\lambda\,\textsf{efs} on every index.

Recall Under Impurity. When authorized vectors are sparse inside the searched structure, ACORN restores reachability by widening neighbor lists, Filtered-DiskANN by stitching label-specific edges, and HoneyBee/SIEVE by over-searching with a larger beam or falling back to linear scans. All four ultimately rely on raising the effective efs, which our cost model (Definition 2.2) shows is linear in latency. Veda reduces the need for inflation by lowering impurity at construction time (copy/merge) and by capping it at execution time through the shared distance bound, rather than by enlarging the candidate set.

9. Conclusion

We presented Veda and EffVeda, two access-aware indexing strategies for vector databases. Both partition data by role combination, organize the resulting blocks in an access-aware lattice, and use copy and merge operations to group co-accessed blocks under a storage budget. Large lattice nodes are indexed with HNSW, while small nodes are scanned linearly. For each role, the methods build a query plan that covers its authorized data with a minimal set of nodes. At query time, coordinated search probes pure nodes first to initialize a global top-kk heap, then uses the resulting distance bound to prune impure nodes. Several directions remain open. Our construction assumes a static dataset and policy; supporting streaming inserts, deletes, and permission revocations without rebuilding the lattice from scratch is a natural next step. Multi-role queries whose authorized region covers a large fraction of 𝒟\mathcal{D} narrow the gap between partition-based and filtered-graph methods, suggesting a hybrid that keeps a global graph alongside the lattice and routes each query based on the size of its authorized region. Looking further, the copy–merge–coordinate framework can extend to richer policies beyond RBAC, such as attribute-based and hierarchical access, etc.
