Appendix A Detailed Introduction of HNSW Index

HNSW is one of the most effective and widely used approximate nearest-neighbor data structures. It organizes vectors into a multi-layer hierarchy in which each layer is a navigable proximity graph (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018). At insertion time, each vector is assigned a maximum level ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0 by sampling from an exponential (geometric) distribution. On every upper layer ℓ>0\ell>0 a node retains up to MM bidirectional links chosen by a diversity-preserving heuristic; on the base layer (ℓ=0\ell=0) the limit is M0≤2​MM_{0}\leq 2M (often configurable in implementations).

To answer a query, HNSW starts at the topmost layer and greedily walks toward the query vector, descending one layer at a time until it reaches the base layer in 𝒪⁡(log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|)\mathcal{O}(\log|{\tt idx}|) expected steps. At the base layer the search switches to a best-first expansion: candidates are kept in a priority queue of capacity efs and expanded in increasing distance, each expansion visiting up to M0M_{0} neighbors. The parameter efs governs the recall–latency trade-off. Counting comparisons, the asymptotic query cost is

𝒪⁡(M​log​|𝚒𝚍𝚡|)+𝒪⁡(efs​log​efs)+𝒪⁡(efs​log​k),\mathcal{O}(M\log|{\tt idx}|)+\mathcal{O}(\textsf{efs}\log\textsf{efs})+\mathcal{O}(\textsf{efs}\log k),

where the three terms account for upper-layer descent, base-layer priority-queue maintenance, and final selection of kk results from the efs candidates.

In role-based settings the comparison-count bound is not the right proxy for latency. When an index is impure for the issuing role, the query must inflate kk to k′=⌈λ​k⌉k^{\prime}=\lceil\lambda k\rceil and efs to ⌈λ​efs⌉\lceil\lambda\,\textsf{efs}\rceil (§2.2), pushing efs into a regime where the base-layer term dominates. Figure 9 sweeps kk (and the corresponding efs=α​k\textsf{efs}=\alpha k) and shows that wall-clock latency grows linearly once kk exceeds a small threshold kok_{o}, not as efs​log⁡efs\textsf{efs}\log\textsf{efs}. The cost model used throughout the paper therefore charges Cθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,efs)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+b​efs+cC_{\theta}({\tt idx},\textsf{efs})=a\log|{\tt idx}|+b\,\textsf{efs}+c (Definition 2.2); Appendix B derives this form from the per-expansion hardware cost and gives the calibration procedure for θ=(a,b,c)\theta=(a,b,c).

Appendix B Selecting the HNSW Search Cost Function

Our partitioning algorithms compare candidate index layouts by their predicted query latency, so they require a closed-form model Cθ​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,efs)C_{\theta}({\tt idx},\textsf{efs}) that maps an index 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} searched with beam width efs to wall-clock time. This appendix justifies the functional form used in Definition 2.2, describes how its coefficients are calibrated, and validates the choice empirically.

B.1. From Asymptotic Complexity to Wall-Clock Latency

The textbook complexity of an HNSW query decomposes into an upper-layer greedy descent of 𝒪⁡(log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|)\mathcal{O}(\log|{\tt idx}|) hops and a base-layer beam search that performs 𝒪⁡(efs)\mathcal{O}(\textsf{efs}) expansions while maintaining a priority queue of capacity efs. Charging each expansion an 𝒪⁡(log⁡efs)\mathcal{O}(\log\textsf{efs}) heap update yields the familiar proxy

C1​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,efs)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+b​efs​log⁡efs+c.C_{1}({\tt idx},\textsf{efs})\;=\;a\log|{\tt idx}|\;+\;b\,\textsf{efs}\log\textsf{efs}\;+\;c.

This expression counts comparisons. It is the wrong currency for latency prediction because the heap update is not where time is spent.

Each base-layer expansion also (i) reads the MM neighbor IDs of the popped node, (ii) fetches the corresponding MM vectors from memory, and (iii) computes MM distances of dd dimensions each. Steps (ii)–(iii) cost 𝒪⁡(M​d)\mathcal{O}(Md) arithmetic operations plus, once the index outgrows the CPU cache, 𝒪⁡(M)\mathcal{O}(M) cache-missing random reads. For a representative configuration (d=128d{=}128, M=16M{=}16, efs=100\textsf{efs}{=}100) a single expansion performs M⋅d=2,048M\!\cdot\!d=2{,}048 multiply–adds and up to 1616 vector fetches, against only log2⁡efs≈7\log_{2}\textsf{efs}\approx 7 heap comparisons. The heap term is therefore two to three orders of magnitude cheaper than the distance term and vanishes into the per-step constant. Since the per-step work does not depend on efs, the base-layer cost is, to first order, linear in the number of expansions:

C2​(𝚒𝚍𝚡,efs)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+b​efs+c.C_{2}({\tt idx},\textsf{efs})\;=\;a\log|{\tt idx}|\;+\;b\,\textsf{efs}\;+\;c.

The constants aa, bb, cc depend on dd, MM, the SIMD width, and the memory hierarchy of the host, none of which are known a priori. We therefore fit them on the deployment machine rather than derive them analytically.

B.2. Calibrating the Cost Function

We isolate the two variable terms with two one-dimensional sweeps (Algorithm 8).

Upper-layer sweep. Fix efs=1\textsf{efs}=1, k=1k=1 and vary |𝚒𝚍𝚡||{\tt idx}|. With a single-slot beam the base layer does negligible work, so the measured latency reflects the greedy descent plus fixed overhead. A least-squares fit of Tsize​(|𝚒𝚍𝚡|)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+c1T_{\textsf{size}}(|{\tt idx}|)=a\log|{\tt idx}|+c_{1} recovers aa.

Base-layer sweep. Fix |𝚒𝚍𝚡|=|𝚒𝚍𝚡0||{\tt idx}|=|{\tt idx}_{0}| and vary efs. We fit both candidates, Tefslin​(efs)=b​efs+c2T_{\textsf{efs}}^{\text{lin}}(\textsf{efs})=b\,\textsf{efs}+c_{2} and Tefslog​(efs)=b′​efs​log⁡efs+c2′T_{\textsf{efs}}^{\text{log}}(\textsf{efs})=b^{\prime}\,\textsf{efs}\log\textsf{efs}+c_{2}^{\prime}, and select whichever attains the higher R2R^{2}.

Combining the intercepts. Each sweep holds the other variable fixed, so each intercept already contains the other term’s contribution at the held value. We remove that contribution from both sides, c(1)=c1−b⋅1c^{(1)}=c_{1}-b\cdot 1 and c(2)=c2−a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡0|c^{(2)}=c_{2}-a\log|{\tt idx}_{0}|, and average the two estimates, c=12​(c(1)+c(2))c=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(c^{(1)}+c^{(2)}\bigr), to damp measurement noise from either sweep.

Figure 10 shows the base-layer sweep on the default configuration (d=128d{=}128, M=16M{=}16). The linear model tracks the measurements across the full range of efs, whereas the efs​log⁡efs\textsf{efs}\log\textsf{efs} model bends upward and over-predicts at large efs—precisely the regime that impure indices enter when λ​efs\lambda\,\textsf{efs} is inflated (Definition 2.2). The linear fit attains R2=0.9938R^{2}=0.9938 versus R2=0.9811R^{2}=0.9811 for the log-linear fit, confirming the hardware argument of §B.1. We therefore adopt

Cθ​(|𝚒𝚍𝚡|,efs)=a​log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+b​efs+c{\,C_{\theta}(|{\tt idx}|,\textsf{efs})\;=\;a\log|{\tt idx}|\;+\;b\,\textsf{efs}\;+\;c\,}

with θ=(a,b,c)\theta=(a,b,c) fitted once per dataset configuration. For the configuration of d=128d{=}128 and M=16M{=}16, the calibrated model is

Cθ​(|𝚒𝚍𝚡|,efs)= 0.0821​log2​|𝚒𝚍𝚡|+ 0.1159​efs+ 2.3110,C_{\theta}(|{\tt idx}|,\textsf{efs})\;=\;0.0821\log_{2}|{\tt idx}|\;+\;0.1159\,\textsf{efs}\;+\;2.3110,

in which the base-layer term dominates for any practical efs while the log⁡|𝚒𝚍𝚡|\log|{\tt idx}| term contributes a small but non-negligible offset. The logarithm base is absorbed into aa; our implementation uses log2\log_{2}.

Appendix C The Optimization Problem

We now give a precise optimization view of the index grouping problem. Given the lattice ℒ𝑒𝑥\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{ex}} with a set of exclusive nodes 𝒩\mathcal{N} and letting 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the set of role subsets (e.g., the set of access control policies, or, the set of combinations of accessible roles) corresponding to 𝒩\mathcal{N}. we build at most one index per τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} by merging and copying exclusive nodes upward in the lattice. The decision variables are:

  • •

    zτ′,τ∈{0,1}z_{\tau^{\prime},\tau}\in\{0,1\}: N⁡(τ′)N(\tau^{\prime}) is included in the index for τ\tau;

  • •

    xτ∈{0,1}x_{\tau}\in\{0,1\}: the index for τ\tau is materialized;

  • •

    yq,τ∈{0,1}y_{q,\tau}\in\{0,1\}: query qq consults the index for τ\tau.

The candidate size of an index for a set τ\tau of roles is sτ=∑τ′zτ′,τ⋅|N⁡(τ′)|.s_{\tau}=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}}z_{\tau^{\prime},\tau}\cdot|N(\tau^{\prime})|. For a query qq with role set q.ρq.\rho, the authorized blocks are 𝒩q={N(τ′):τ′∩q.ρ≠∅}\mathcal{N}_{q}=\{N(\tau^{\prime}):\tau^{\prime}\cap q.\rho\neq\emptyset\}. If the query uses indices {τ:yq,τ=1}\{\tau:y_{q,\tau}=1\} to look for its nearest neighbors, the query-time cost is:

Cost(q)=∑τ:yq,τ=1logsτ+α∑N⁡(τ′)∈𝒩q|N(τ′)|⋅∏τ:yq,τ=1(1−zτ′,τ)\textsf{Cost}(q)=\sum_{\tau:y_{q,\tau}=1}\log s_{\tau}+\alpha\sum_{N(\tau^{\prime})\in\mathcal{N}_{q}}\,|N(\tau^{\prime})|\cdot\prod_{\tau:y_{q,\tau}=1}(1-z_{\tau^{\prime},\tau})

The second term inflates the cost proportionally to any portion of qq’s authorized blocks that are not covered by the selected indices.

The overall workload objective is:

(7) minx,z,y∑q∈𝒬q.ω(∑τ∈𝒯yq,τlogsτ+α∑N⁡(τ′)∈𝒩q|N(τ′)|⋅∏τ:yq,τ=1(1−zτ′,τ))\min_{x,z,y}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}q.\omega\left(\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}y_{q,\tau}\log s_{\tau}+\alpha\sum_{N(\tau^{\prime})\in\mathcal{N}_{q}}\,|N(\tau^{\prime})|\cdot\prod_{\tau:y_{q,\tau}=1}(1-z_{\tau^{\prime},\tau})\right)

subject to:

(8) ∀τ′,τ:zτ′,τ≤xτ\displaystyle\forall\tau^{\prime},\tau:\quad z_{\tau^{\prime},\tau}\leq x_{\tau} (include in materialized index)
(9) ∀τ′,τ:0≤zτ′,τ≤aτ′,τ\displaystyle\forall\tau^{\prime},\tau:\quad 0\leq z_{\tau^{\prime},\tau}\leq a_{\tau^{\prime},\tau} aτ′,τ=1​ if ​τ′∩τ≠∅​ else ​0\displaystyle a_{\tau^{\prime},\tau}=1\text{ if }\tau^{\prime}\cap\tau\neq\emptyset\text{ else }0
(10) ∀τ:sτ=∑τ′zτ′,τ​|N⁡(τ′)|\displaystyle\forall\tau:\quad s_{\tau}=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}}z_{\tau^{\prime},\tau}|N(\tau^{\prime})|
(11) ∑τxτ​sτ≤β​|𝒟|\displaystyle\sum_{\tau}x_{\tau}s_{\tau}\leq\beta|\mathcal{D}| (storage budget)

All variables are binary; β≥1\beta\geq 1 bounds the storage amplification. Because sτs_{\tau} and the cost expression contain products and logs, the objective (7) is non-convex.

A common simplification is to pre-enumerate a finite catalogue 𝒢c\mathcal{G}_{c} of valid groups (from merge/copy operations), treat |g||g| as a constant, and decide which groups to index. Let xg,yq,g,uq,𝒩x_{g},y_{q,g},u_{q,\mathcal{N}} be binary variables as in §3. With log⁡|g|\log|g| constant, the objective becomes linear:

(12) min⁡∑q∈𝒬x,y,u⁡q.ω⁡(∑g∈𝒢cyq,g​log⁡|g|+α​∑N⁡(τ′)∈𝒩quq,N⁡(τ′)​|N⁡(τ′)|)\min_{x,y,u}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}q.\omega\left(\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{c}}y_{q,g}\log|g|+\alpha\sum_{N(\tau^{\prime})\in\mathcal{N}_{q}}u_{q,N(\tau^{\prime})}|N(\tau^{\prime})|\right)

subject to:

(13) yq,g\displaystyle y_{q,g} ≤xg\displaystyle\leq x_{g} ∀q,g\displaystyle\forall q,g

Equations (12)–(16) define a 0–1 MILP.

Enumerating 𝒢c\mathcal{G}_{c} reduces the problem to a MILP, but scale remains a challenge: |𝒢c||\mathcal{G}_{c}| can reach tens of thousands; yq,gy_{q,g} spans millions of binaries for realistic workloads, and runtimes remain prohibitive. Moreover, fixed catalogues cannot adapt to shifting role distributions or data updates.

Appendix D Copy Operation Dominance

To justify prioritizing copy operations, we compare their effect on query workloads. Let Cost​(Q,ℒ)\textsf{Cost}(Q,\mathcal{L}) denote the cost of evaluating a workload QQ over lattice ℒ\mathcal{L}. Consider a child node Nc=N⁡(τc)N_{c}=N(\tau_{c}) and an ancestor Na=N⁡(τa)N_{a}=N(\tau_{a}). Let ℒ𝑐𝑜𝑝𝑦\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{copy}} be the lattice where NcN_{c} is copied into NaN_{a} (so both remain), and ℒ𝑚𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑒\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{merge}} the lattice where NcN_{c} is merged into NaN_{a} (and removed). The following result shows that copying never performs worse than merging, and may strictly improve cost for workloads that isolate NcN_{c}.

Theorem D.1 (Copy Dominance).

Suppose both copying and merging NcN_{c} into NaN_{a} yield positive cost reduction for queries that involve roles in τa\tau_{a}. Then the following hold for all queries in QQ:

  • •

    If a query accesses only NcN_{c}, then Cost​(Q,ℒ𝑐𝑜𝑝𝑦)<Cost​(Q,ℒ𝑚𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑒).\textsf{Cost}(Q,\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{copy}})<\textsf{Cost}(Q,\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{merge}}).

  • •

    If a query access both NcN_{c} and NaN_{a}, then Cost​(Q,ℒ𝑐𝑜𝑝𝑦)=Cost​(Q,ℒ𝑚𝑒𝑟𝑔𝑒).\textsf{Cost}(Q,\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{copy}})=\textsf{Cost}(Q,\mathcal{L}_{\mathit{merge}}).

Appendix E Supplementary Algorithms for Veda

This section collects the subroutines invoked by Algorithms 2 and 3 in §4 and the finalization phase referenced from the algorithm overview.

E.1. Copy-Phase Helpers

Algorithm 9 provides get_pairs, get_benefit, and get_diff as called from Algorithm 2. get_pairs (re)scores only the child–ancestor pairs whose ancestor was touched by the previous copy; get_benefit evaluates Equation (3) for a candidate copy; and get_diff computes the change in a single role’s plan cost when its query plan switches from the current cover to one that uses the enlarged ancestor.

E.2. Merge-Phase Helpers

Algorithm 10 supplies the merge-phase analogues called from Algorithm 3. get_merge_benefit differs from the copy case in that it must also charge the impurity introduced for roles that previously read the child as a pure node.

E.3. Phase 3: Finalization

After the merge phase, any remaining nodes that are not indexable are decomposed back into exclusive blocks for linear scan. As there might be duplicated data between these groups that has reclaimed storage, identify nodes that are “super impure” to issue queries and create copies of the pure parts to utilize the freed budget.

Algorithm 11 formalizes this procedure. The algorithm first computes each node NN’s reference count in ℒ\mathcal{L}, i.e., the number of roles that access a node NN, denoted 𝑟𝑒𝑓⁡[N]\mathit{ref}[N]. Then, for each role rr, the algorithm computes its impurity of each node in QP​[r]\textsf{QP}[r] with the pure part of NN for rr, denoted 𝑝𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑥\mathit{pure}^{\mathit{ex}}. If this pure part is smaller than NN, NN is impure for rr, and the pair is added to a candidate list with an impurity score. Candidates are processed in decreasing impurity order. Before refining a candidate, the algorithm computes the additional copy size 𝑐𝑜𝑝𝑦s\mathit{copy}_{s} by counting only exclusive blocks in 𝑝𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑥\mathit{pure}^{\mathit{ex}} that have not already been copied by earlier refinements. If the remaining budget is sufficient, the algorithm materializes each exclusive block into a standalone node that can be used directly in the query plan. When the block is already standalone in ℒ\mathcal{L}, the algorithm reuses it without spending budget. Otherwise, the block is copied into ℒ\mathcal{L}: it keeps its original key if that key is free, and uses a renamed key if the original key is already occupied by a non-standalone node. The query plan QP​[r]\textsf{QP}[r] is redirected to these materialized blocks, and the original impure node is removed from QP​[r]\textsf{QP}[r]. When this update makes 𝑟𝑒𝑓⁡[N]=0\mathit{ref}[N]=0, the node is not referenced by any query andis safe to delete from ℒ\mathcal{L} to reclaim the storage.

Appendix F Supplementary Algorithms for EffVeda

F.1. Copy with Valid Partitions of Sizes over Two

Guided by Lemma 5.4, when allowing the number of ancestors in the valid partitions to be higher than two, EffVeda enumerates ancestor subsets at each layer ℓ\ell in increasing cardinality η\eta (starting from 2), verifies validity and storage feasibility, and evaluates f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot). It then selects BPc\textsf{BP}_{c}—the valid partition with maximal benefit under the storage budget. This greedy bottom-up procedure confines exploration to local, purity-preserving operations while respecting the global SA constraint. The algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 12.

F.2. Finding the Best Valid Partition

Algorithm 13 returns, for a child node and a target partition size η\eta, the valid partition of its ancestor set that maximizes the benefit of Equation (5) under the remaining SA budget. It is the subroutine invoked by Algorithm 12 and by the η=2\eta=2 search in §5.

Appendix G Query Answering Algorithms

This section collects the algorithms used by §6. The starred notation in the pseudocode, such as ℐ∗​(r)\mathcal{I}^{*}(r) and 𝒰∗​(r)\mathcal{U}^{*}(r), denotes the selected indices and leftover vectors in the query plan QP​(r)\textsf{QP}(r).

G.1. Detailed Top-kk Query Execution

Given a query q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) and a query plan QP​(r)=(ℐ​(r),𝒰​(r))\textsf{QP}(r)=(\mathcal{I}(r),\mathcal{U}(r)), the baseline execution strategy searches every selected component independently. Leftover vectors in 𝒰⁡(r)\mathcal{U}(r) are stored by block and scanned linearly. For each HNSW index 𝚒𝚍𝚡∈ℐ⁡(r){\tt idx}\in\mathcal{I}(r), the query uses standard top-kk search when 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} is pure for rr. If 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} is impure, the query inflates the request size to k′=⌈λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r​k⌉k^{\prime}=\lceil\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}k\rceil, where λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}} is defined in Equation 1, and filters the returned candidates against 𝒟⁡(r)\mathcal{D}(r). The final answer is the top-kk closest authorized vectors after merging the filtered HNSW results and the linear-scan results.

Coordinated search improves on this baseline by using the pure indices and leftovers to establish a global distance boundary before fully inflating impure-index search. Algorithm 7 first initializes the global result heap 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS} using 𝒰∗​(r)\mathcal{U}^{*}(r) and pure indices. For each impure index, it runs an uninflated HNSW search, filters authorized candidates, and merges only candidates that can beat the current kk-th global result. If the local kk-th result is already farther than the global kk-th result, the algorithm stops exploring that impure index. Otherwise, it continues the base-layer traversal with an inflated beam and merges the newly found authorized vectors.

G.2. Continued Base-Layer Search on Impure Indices

Algorithm 17 gives the base-layer (layer-00) HNSW traversal used inside Algorithm 7 when an impure index must be searched under the global distance bound. The traversal carries the current global kk-th distance dk(g)d_{k}^{(g)} from 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS} as an admission threshold: a neighbor is pushed onto the candidate heap only if it can still enter the global top-kk, and the loop terminates as soon as the best remaining candidate is farther than dk(g)d_{k}^{(g)}. Authorization is checked before a vector is admitted to the local result heap, so unauthorized vectors steer the traversal but never reach 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS}.

G.3. Accuracy Analysis of Inflated-kk Search

We formalize when inflated-kk search over an impure index returns the true authorized top-kk. For a query q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) on an impure index 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx}, the goal is to retrieve the kk closest vectors in 𝒟r​(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}_{r}({\tt idx}) under dist​(⋅,⋅)\textsf{dist}(\cdot,\cdot). Because unauthorized vectors may appear before authorized ones in the unfiltered ranking, the kk-th authorized vector can occur after position kk.

Definition G.1 (Authorized Position Threshold).

Let u1,u2,…u_{1},u_{2},\ldots denote all vectors in 𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}({\tt idx}) sorted by increasing dist​(𝐱,ui)\textsf{dist}(\mathbf{x},u_{i}). Define

τr=min⁡{t∣|{u1,…,ut}∩𝒟r​(𝚒𝚍𝚡)|≥k},\tau_{r}=\min\Bigl\{t\mid\bigl|\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{t}\}\cap\mathcal{D}_{r}({\tt idx})\bigr|\geq k\Bigr\},

i.e., the position in the full unfiltered ranking where the kk-th authorized vector appears.

Retrieving at least the first τr\tau_{r} true unfiltered neighbors is therefore sufficient to include all kk authorized nearest neighbors.

Assumption 1 (HNSW Top-tt Success Condition).

For any index 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} and any integer t≥1t\geq 1, there exists a non-decreasing function f⁡(t)f(t) such that running HNSW on 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx} with parameter efs≥f⁡(t)\textsf{efs}\geq f(t) returns the true top-tt nearest neighbors by distance with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

This assumption abstracts the empirical behavior that larger efs values yield higher HNSW recall. In our implementation, f⁡(t)=α​tf(t)=\alpha t with a small constant α\alpha (e.g., 5≤α≤105\leq\alpha\leq 10) satisfies the condition with high probability.

Theorem G.2 (Accuracy of Inflated-kk Search).

Fix a query q=(𝐱,r)q=(\mathbf{x},r) on an impure index 𝚒𝚍𝚡{\tt idx}. Let the search retrieve the true top-k′k^{\prime} unfiltered neighbors of 𝐱\mathbf{x} from 𝒟⁡(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}({\tt idx}) with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for some k′≥τrk^{\prime}\geq\tau_{r}. Then, after filtering unauthorized vectors from this result set, the remaining vectors contain exactly the true top-kk authorized neighbors of 𝐱\mathbf{x} in 𝒟r​(𝚒𝚍𝚡)\mathcal{D}_{r}({\tt idx}), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Proof.

By definition of τr\tau_{r}, the kk-th authorized neighbor ak∈𝒟r​(𝚒𝚍𝚡)a_{k}\in\mathcal{D}_{r}({\tt idx}) appears within the first τr\tau_{r} elements of the true unfiltered ranking. If the algorithm returns the true top-k′k^{\prime} unfiltered neighbors with k′≥τrk^{\prime}\geq\tau_{r}, then all u1,…,uτru_{1},\ldots,u_{\tau_{r}} are included. Filtering unauthorized vectors from this set retains all authorized neighbors up to aka_{k}. No authorized vector after position τr\tau_{r} can precede aka_{k} in distance. Hence, the first kk vectors after filtering are exactly the true top-kk authorized neighbors, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. ∎

Corollary G.3 (Inflation Rule).

Under Assumption 1, Theorem G.2 holds if the search parameters satisfy k′≥τrk^{\prime}\geq\tau_{r} and efs′≥f⁡(k′)\textsf{efs}^{\prime}\geq f(k^{\prime}).

In practice, τr\tau_{r} is unknown. Coordinated search estimates an inflation factor λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r≥1\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}\geq 1 from the observed relation between the local impure-index ranking and the global result heap 𝖱𝖲\mathsf{RS}. Setting

k′=⌈λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r⋅k⌉,efs′=⌈λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r⋅efs⌉k^{\prime}=\lceil\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}\cdot k\rceil,\qquad\textsf{efs}^{\prime}=\lceil\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}}\cdot\textsf{efs}\rceil

grows the target size and the HNSW beam together. If the chosen λ𝚒𝚍𝚡r\lambda^{r}_{{\tt idx}} is large enough that k′≥τrk^{\prime}\geq\tau_{r}, Corollary G.3 guarantees that filtering the returned set yields the exact authorized top-kk with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Appendix H Complementary Evaluations

H.1. Supplementary Results for Exp 7.3: Varying Indexing Thresholds

This section reports the additional results for Exp 7.3 in §7. In the main text, we show the sensitivity of QPS to the indexing threshold Λ\Lambda at SA=1.1=1.1. Tables 7 and 8 repeat the same evaluation with larger storage budgets, SA=1.3=1.3 and SA=1.5=1.5. The results follow the same trend: varying Λ\Lambda changes QPS only mildly, confirming that the proposed methods are robust to the exact indexing threshold.

H.2. Supplementary Results for Exp 7.3: Impacts of efs

We provide evaluation resutls on the PAPER and AMZN datasets, as a complement to Exp 7.3 in §7. As on SIFT-1M, increasing efs lowers QPS for all methods because each HNSW search expands a wider beam. The relative trends are consistent across datasets. Oracle achieves the highest QPS on all datasets, and Veda and EffVeda maintain high QPS over most of the evaluations.

Appendix I Supporting Dynamic Workloads

The construction in §4–§5 assumes a static dataset and policy. We sketch here how the lattice absorbs insertions, deletions, and updates without a full rebuild.

Data updates. Every vector vv belongs to exactly one exclusive block N𝑒𝑥​(τ)N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau), and the container map Φ\Phi (§6.1) records the set of lattice nodes that physically hold that block. Insert​(v,τ)\textsf{Insert}(v,\tau) adds vv to each node in Φ​(N𝑒𝑥​(τ))\Phi(N^{\mathit{ex}}(\tau)); Delete​(v)\textsf{Delete}(v) removes it from the same set; Update​(v,v′)\textsf{Update}(v,v^{\prime}) is a delete followed by an insert. Indexed nodes use HNSW’s native incremental insertion (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018) and tombstone deletion; leftover nodes are arrays with 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) update.

Policy updates. Granting or revoking role rr on vv moves vv from block τ\tau to τ∪{r}\tau\cup\{r\} or τ∖{r}\tau\setminus\{r\}; only nodes in the symmetric difference Φ⁡(τ)​△​Φ​(τ′)\Phi(\tau)\,\triangle\,\Phi(\tau^{\prime}) are touched, and a previously unseen destination block is created as a fresh leftover node. Adding a role is metadata only. Dropping role rr relabels every block τ∋r\tau\ni r to τ∖{r}\tau\setminus\{r\} and merges blocks that collide; node contents are unchanged, so no HNSW index is rebuilt.

Optimization. These operations keep the layout correct. Every authorized vector stays reachable through some node in QP​(r)\textsf{QP}(r), and coordinated search post-filters any newly impure node—but let it drift from the QA optimum as block sizes and impurities change. We restore optimality lazily: when a node crosses the threshold Λ\Lambda or its size/impurity drifts beyond a slack, we re-run copy/merge on that node and its lattice neighbors only. Only after large policy changes (e.g., DropRole), we re-run EffVeda in full.

Appendix J Detailed Related Work

This appendix expands the qualitative comparison of §8 into a method-level survey. The unifying question is where a system pays for the access predicate: before ANN search (pre-filtering), during graph traversal (in-index filtering), through additional materialized sub-indexes (workload-aware selection), or through an access-control-aware partitioning of the data itself. We organize the discussion along that axis and, for each method, state how Veda and EffVeda differ.

J.1. Access-Control Foundations

Classical database access control defines policy models such as DAC, MAC, and RBAC and studies their enforcement, administration, and auditing in relational systems (Bertino et al., 2011). That literature fixes the security semantics a vector store must satisfy but says nothing about ANN-specific concerns: approximate traversal, candidate-set inflation, or coordination across several indices. Recent benchmarks for organization-scale retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020), e.g., OrgAccess (Sanyal et al., 2025), confirm that policy-compliant retrieval over embedding stores is now a first-class requirement and motivate the problem we study.

J.2. General-Purpose ANN Indexing

Unconstrained ANN indices are the primitives every system below builds on. FAISS (Johnson et al., 2019) popularized partition- and compression-based indices (IVF, product quantization) that assign vectors to coarse clusters and probe a subset of inverted lists. HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018) builds a multi-layer navigable small-world graph and answers queries by greedy descent from sparse upper layers to a dense base layer. DiskANN (Subramanya et al., 2019) introduces the Vamana graph for high-recall billion-scale search with most of the index resident on SSD. ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020) combines partition pruning with anisotropic vector quantization for large-scale maximum-inner-product search. All four assume a single global search space; they are orthogonal to access control and appear in Veda only as the per-group index implementation.

J.3. Filtered and Category-Aware Vector Search

Filtered ANN attaches attributes to vectors and returns nearest neighbors that satisfy a predicate. The generic strategies—pre-filtering (materialize the matching set, then search it), post-filtering (search globally, then discard non-matching results), and result-set filtering (test the predicate before admitting a candidate to the top-kk)—are easy to layer onto any index but fail in opposite regimes: pre-filtering degenerates to a scan when the predicate is broad, and post-filtering must over-search heavily when the predicate is selective. The systems below each move the predicate deeper into the index to avoid that “unhappy middle.”

Filtered-DiskANN (Gollapudi et al., 2023) makes the Vamana graph label-aware. FilteredVamana inserts points incrementally and prunes edges using both geometry and label overlap; StitchedVamana builds one Vamana graph per label, overlays their edge sets into a single graph, and prunes high-degree nodes. The result remains a single SSD-friendly graph, so storage stays near SA≈1{\approx}1, but the relevant label universe must be fixed at construction time. RBAC roles satisfy that assumption, yet a role’s visible set is the union of many label-specific subgraphs; Filtered-DiskANN has no mechanism to stitch those subgraphs at query time, so a role with broad access still falls back to over-search on the overlaid graph. Veda avoids this by materializing the union explicitly as a group when the storage budget allows.

UNG (Cai et al., 2024) augments a graph index with a separate label-navigating graph that encodes containment among label sets, so equality, subset, and overlap predicates can prune vectors that cannot match before any distance is computed. The predicate model is richer than Filtered-DiskANN’s but remains a category-search model: it accelerates “find vectors whose labels contain LL,” not “find vectors visible to role rr across all of rr’s permissions.” Veda’s role-subset lattice plays the analogous navigational role for RBAC, but its nodes are physical index groups rather than logical label sets.

ACORN (Patel et al., 2024) targets predicate-agnostic hybrid search on HNSW. For a query predicate pp, search is confined to the subgraph induced by vectors satisfying pp; because filtering can disconnect that subgraph, ACORN-γ\gamma widens neighbor lists by a factor γ\gamma at construction time (with predicate-agnostic pruning), and ACORN-11 keeps construction close to vanilla HNSW but expands one- and two-hop neighbors at query time. Both variants restore reachability by exposing a denser neighborhood before the predicate is applied. ACORN handles arbitrary predicates and therefore cannot exploit that RBAC predicates are few, fixed, and heavily overlapping; in our setting its γ\gamma-expansion pays a uniform construction tax for flexibility Veda does not need.

SIEVE (Li et al., 2025) is the filtered-ANN system closest to our optimization. Rather than modify traversal, it selects a workload-aware collection of HNSW sub-indexes under a memory budget and routes each query to one of them. For a sub-index IhI_{h} whose filter hh subsumes a query filter ff, SIEVE models memory as

S⁡(Ih)=M⋅card⁡(h),S(I_{h})=M\cdot\operatorname{card}(h),

and indexed search cost as

C⁡(Ih,𝑠𝑒𝑓,w,f)=log⁡(card⁡(h))⋅𝑠𝑒𝑓⋅(card⁡(h)card⁡(f))cor⁡(w,f,h),C(I_{h},\mathit{sef},w,f)=\log(\operatorname{card}(h))\cdot\mathit{sef}\cdot\left(\frac{\operatorname{card}(h)}{\operatorname{card}(f)}\right)^{\operatorname{cor}(w,f,h)},

where card⁡(⋅)\operatorname{card}(\cdot) is filter cardinality, 𝑠𝑒𝑓\mathit{sef} is the HNSW search parameter, and cor⁡(w,f,h)\operatorname{cor}(w,f,h) captures query–filter correlation inside IhI_{h}. Brute-force search costs Cb​f​(f)=card⁡(f)C_{bf}(f)=\operatorname{card}(f) up to a calibration constant, and a built collection ℐ\mathcal{I} serves ff at

C⁡(ℐ,f)=min⁡(Cb​f​(f),minIh∈ℐ⁡C⁡(Ih,f)).C(\mathcal{I},f)=\min\!\left(C_{bf}(f),\;\min_{I_{h}\in\mathcal{I}}C(I_{h},f)\right).

Given a historical workload ℋ={(hi,ci)}\mathcal{H}=\{(h_{i},c_{i})\} and budget BB, SIEVE solves

min⁡∑(hi,ci)∈ℋℐ⁡ci​C​(ℐ,hi)s.t.I∞∈ℐ,∑Ih∈ℐS⁡(Ih)≤B\min_{\mathcal{I}}\;\sum_{(h_{i},c_{i})\in\mathcal{H}}c_{i}\,C(\mathcal{I},h_{i})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad I_{\infty}\in\mathcal{I},\;\sum_{I_{h}\in\mathcal{I}}S(I_{h})\leq B

greedily, adding at each step the sub-index with the largest marginal cost-reduction per memory unit, and organizes the result into a Hasse diagram over filter subsumption so that a BFS from the root I∞I_{\infty} finds the smallest subsuming sub-index (any node whose filter does not subsume ff prunes its entire subtree). Two design choices separate SIEVE from Veda. First, SIEVE serves each query from one sub-index; an RBAC role whose visible set is the union of several disjoint blocks must either fall back to I∞I_{\infty} or accept an impure superset. EffVeda instead probes multiple authorized indices and shares a global distance bound across them. Second, SIEVE’s search space is “which sub-indexes to add”; Veda’s is “which blocks to merge and which to copy,” which can also reduce the number of indices a role touches without spending budget.

J.4. Access-Control-Aware Vector Search

Production deployments typically sit at one of two extremes. A global index with row-level filtering stores every vector once (SA=1{=}1) and enforces access control by post-filtering, so queries spend most of their beam on unauthorized vectors whenever the role is selective. An oracle index builds the ideal pure HNSW graph for each access predicate known at construction time, e.g., a role or user visibility set; this makes search trivial but duplicates every shared vector and becomes unmanageable when permissions overlap heavily. Veda treats these as the two endpoints of the SA/QA curve (§2.2) and searches the interior.

HoneyBee (Zhong et al., 2025) is the closest prior work. It casts RBAC vector search as a dynamic partitioning problem: overlapping partitions replicate vectors selectively, using the “thin waist” of RBAC roles to balance storage, latency, and recall. Its per-user latency model is

Cu​(Π,ui,𝑒𝑓s)=∑j∈APmin​(ui,Π)log⁡(|πj|)⋅(a⋅𝑒𝑓s+b),C_{u}(\Pi,u_{i},\mathit{ef}_{s})=\sum_{j\in\mathrm{AP}_{\min}(u_{i},\Pi)}\log(|\pi_{j}|)\cdot(a\cdot\mathit{ef}_{s}+b),

where Π\Pi is the partitioning, APmin​(ui,Π)\mathrm{AP}_{\min}(u_{i},\Pi) is the minimal set of partitions that cover uiu_{i}’s visible data, and 𝑒𝑓s\mathit{ef}_{s} is the HNSW search parameter. HoneyBee pairs this with a selectivity-based recall model, formulates partitioning as a constrained MINLP, and—because the exact problem is NP-hard—solves it with a greedy split heuristic that repeatedly divides role groups when the predicted latency gain justifies the storage cost.

Veda shares HoneyBee’s objective but differs on three axes. (i) Search space. HoneyBee moves top-down by splitting; Veda moves over the role-subset lattice with both copy and merge, so it can reach layouts—e.g., two blocks merged into one pure group for a frequent role pair—that no sequence of splits produces. (ii) Cost model. HoneyBee charges log⁡|πj|⋅(a​𝑒𝑓s+b)\log|\pi_{j}|\cdot(a\,\mathit{ef}_{s}+b) per partition; Veda uses the hardware-calibrated CθC_{\theta} of Definition 2.2, whose linear-efs term is the quantity the optimizer actually manipulates through impurity λ\lambda. (iii) Execution. HoneyBee searches each partition in APmin\mathrm{AP}_{\min} independently. EffVeda runs them in a coordinated schedule in which pure partitions are probed first and their top-kk distances become an admission threshold for the beam on impure partitions and residual linear scans, so the inflated λ​efs\lambda\,\textsf{efs} of Definition 2.2 is paid only on the fraction of impure candidates that survive the bound.
